entry_json.definition: on the following occasion that something happens; used with no preposition before it, and it can open a sentence or close one
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Next time I take the test I am going to spend far longer on the writing section.
example_sentences: I ran out of time in the reading paper, so next time I will practise with a clock in front of me.
The bus was full, so we waited for the next one and got seats next time.

contexts.text: Next time I take the test I am going to spend far longer on the writing section.
Next time we visit, we'll book the hotel much earlier.
Governments say that next time a shortage occurs they will be better prepared.

confusables.difference: Last time looks back at the previous occasion; next time looks forward to the coming one. Compare 'Last time I failed' with 'Next time I will pass'.
minimal_pair: Last time I took the test I was too slow.
Next time I take the test I will be faster.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'in the next time' or 'on next time'. The phrase takes no preposition: 'Next time, I will...'.

entry_json.definition: during the week after this one; used with no preposition, and normally with a future form
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have my speaking test next week, so I am practising every evening.
example_sentences: We are moving into the new flat next week once the paperwork is signed.
The results come out next week, which is why everyone in the class is nervous.

contexts.text: I have my speaking test next week, so I am practising every evening.
The report is due next week, so the team is working late.
Next week the new timetable comes into force across the whole network.

confusables.difference: 'Next week' means the week after this one. 'The next week' means a period of seven days counted from now, and usually follows a verb: 'She stayed for the next week.'
minimal_pair: I stayed at home for the next week.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'in next week' or 'on next week'. Say simply 'next week'.

entry_json.definition: during the year after this one; used with no preposition, usually with a future form
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am hoping to start my master's degree next year if my band score is high enough.
example_sentences: My brother finishes secondary school next year and wants to study engineering.
The company plans to open two more branches next year.

contexts.text: I am hoping to start my master's degree next year if my band score is high enough.
Next year the city will introduce a congestion charge in the centre.
Spending on renewable energy is forecast to rise again next year.

confusables.difference: Last year points backwards and takes a past tense; next year points forwards and takes a future form.
minimal_pair: Last year I worked in a cafe.
Next year I will work in a hospital.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'in next year'. Also avoid the past tense with it: not 'Next year I went', but 'Next year I will go'.

entry_json.definition: the short question form of 'next year', used on its own to check or query a plan somebody has just mentioned; the rest of the sentence is left out because both speakers already know it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: 'We're thinking of moving.' 'Next year?' 'No, probably the year after.'
example_sentences: 'I'd like to take the test again.' 'Next year?' 'Sooner, I hope.'
'They're opening a second campus.' 'Next year?' 'That's the plan, yes.'

contexts.text: 'We're thinking of moving.' 'Next year?' 'No, probably the year after.'
'I'm going to retake it.' 'Next year?' 'As soon as I can, actually.'

confusables.difference: The short form only works when the listener can fill in the missing words from what was just said. In writing, or when the idea is new, you need the full question.

entry_json.avoid: This elliptical question belongs to conversation only. Never use a bare fragment like this in Task 1 or Task 2 writing.

entry_json.definition: used to say that something is very probably true; it sits before the verb or at the start of the clause and works as a hedge, not as proof
entry_json.own_context_sentence: No doubt the government will point to the falling unemployment figures.
example_sentences: The exam was difficult, and no doubt many candidates will resit it.
There is no doubt that air quality in the city has improved since the ban.

contexts.text: No doubt the government will point to the falling unemployment figures.
She's no doubt already at the station waiting for us.
There is no doubt that the sample was too small to support the conclusion.

confusables.difference: 'Undoubtedly' claims something is certain. 'No doubt' is softer and often signals a point you are about to argue against: 'No doubt costs will rise, but...'.
minimal_pair: No doubt costs will rise, but the benefit is greater.

confusables.difference: Doubtless is a formal one-word adverb with the same job; no doubt is the everyday version and is safer in speech.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'no doubt that the answer is...' when you mean certainty. Bare 'no doubt' concedes a point; for full certainty use 'There is no doubt that...'.

entry_json.definition: not any more; it goes between the subject and the main verb, or after the first auxiliary or 'be'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Coal is no longer the main source of electricity in the country.
example_sentences: Many families no longer cook from scratch during the working week.
The library no longer charges for late returns.

contexts.text: Coal is no longer the main source of electricity in the country.
Students no longer need to visit the library to borrow a text.
I no longer drive to work because parking became impossible.

confusables.difference: Same meaning, different position and register. 'No longer' is written and goes mid-sentence; 'not any longer' is spoken and goes at the end.
minimal_pair: He doesn't work here any longer.

confusables.difference: 'No more' is about quantity, 'no longer' is about time. 'There is no more coal' is amount; 'coal is no longer used' is time.

entry_json.avoid: Do not add a second negative: not 'doesn't no longer work'. 'No longer' is already the negative.

entry_json.definition: used to say that something stays true whatever the degree; the pattern is 'no matter how' + adjective or adverb + subject + verb
entry_json.own_context_sentence: No matter how carefully you plan, some part of the journey always goes wrong.
example_sentences: No matter how hard she revised, the listening section stayed her weakest paper.
No matter how expensive housing becomes, people continue to move to the capital.
collocations: no matter how long it takes
no matter how much sth costs

contexts.text: No matter how carefully you plan, some part of the journey always goes wrong.
No matter how strict the law is, enforcement decides whether it works.
No matter how good the equipment is, it is useless without training.

confusables.difference: 'However' + adjective does the same job in formal writing: 'however carefully you plan'. 'No matter how' is the everyday version and is common in speech.
minimal_pair: No matter how carefully you plan...

confusables.difference: 'How' asks about degree, 'what' about the thing itself. 'No matter how much it costs' versus 'No matter what it costs'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not put an object after 'how' when an adjective belongs there. Say 'no matter how difficult it is', not 'no matter how it is difficult'.

entry_json.definition: used to say that something will be true whatever happens; it can stand at the end of a sentence on its own in speech
entry_json.own_context_sentence: No matter what the critics say, the museum is still the most visited building in the city.
example_sentences: I am going to sit the test in March, no matter what.
No matter what career they choose, graduates need to keep learning.

contexts.text: No matter what the critics say, the museum is still the most visited building in the city.
I'm going to finish the course, no matter what.
No matter what the survey shows, the sample was too small to generalise from.

confusables.difference: 'Whatever' is the single-word formal equivalent: 'whatever the critics say'. 'No matter what' is more common in speech and slightly more emphatic.
'What' concerns the event or the thing; 'how' concerns the degree.

entry_json.avoid: The tail-end version, 'I'll do it no matter what', is spoken. In Task 2 put the clause first and complete it: 'No matter what the outcome is, ...'.

entry_json.definition: the opening of a concession pattern; it must be followed by a question word such as what, how, who, when or where, then a clause
entry_json.own_context_sentence: No matter which option the council chooses, some residents will object.
example_sentences: No matter where you live in the country, broadband should reach the same speed.
No matter when the meeting is held, somebody cannot attend.

contexts.text: No matter which option the council chooses, some residents will object.
No matter where you sit in that lecture hall, you can't hear properly.
No matter who conducts the study, the same variables must be controlled.

confusables.difference: 'It doesn't matter' is a complete sentence and says something is unimportant. 'No matter...' is a linker that opens a clause and must be followed by a question word.
minimal_pair: No matter what happens, I'll be there.

entry_json.avoid: 'No matter' cannot stand alone before a noun. Not 'no matter the weather' in formal writing; write 'no matter what the weather is' or 'whatever the weather'.

entry_json.definition: used before a number or amount to say that it is small, or before a noun to say that something is only that and nothing better; it sits directly before the quantity
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The scheme cost no more than two per cent of the annual transport budget.
example_sentences: The walk from the station takes no more than ten minutes.
Critics dismissed the plan as no more than a publicity exercise.

contexts.text: The scheme cost no more than two per cent of the annual transport budget.
It's no more than a ten-minute walk from my flat to the office.
For many households the rise was no more than a few pounds a month.

confusables.difference: 'Not more than' is a neutral upper limit, like a rule. 'No more than' adds the writer's opinion that the amount is small.
minimal_pair: Applicants may submit not more than three samples.
The delay was no more than three minutes.

confusables.difference: 'No less than' emphasises that a number is surprisingly large; 'no more than' that it is small.
minimal_pair: No less than 80 per cent voted.
No more than 8 per cent voted.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it for a plain maximum in a rule or instruction; 'not more than' or 'a maximum of' is clearer there.

entry_json.definition: an emphatic refusal or a strong statement that something is impossible; used alone as an answer, or before a clause
entry_json.own_context_sentence: 'Could you finish it tonight?' 'No way, I've got an exam in the morning.'
example_sentences: There's no way I could afford to live in the city centre on that salary.
'They finished the whole project in a week.' 'No way!'
collocations: there's no way sb could do sth
no way am I doing sth

contexts.text: 'Could you finish it tonight?' 'No way, I've got an exam in the morning.'
There's no way I could afford to live in the city centre on that salary.

confusables.difference: Same refusal, different register. 'Certainly not' is polite and usable with strangers; 'no way' is informal and can sound rude to someone senior.
This is the formal written equivalent. Task 2 needs that form, not the idiom.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'no way' in Task 1 or Task 2. In writing use 'it would be impossible to...' or 'this is unlikely to...'.

entry_json.definition: not from now on, when something used to be true; it goes at the end of the clause, and the 'not' is usually inside a contraction
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I used to take the bus, but I don't any longer because the fares went up.
example_sentences: She doesn't live with her parents any longer.
'Do they still make that model?' 'Not any longer, I'm afraid.'

contexts.text: I used to take the bus, but I don't any longer because the fares went up.
She doesn't live with her parents any longer.

confusables.difference: Identical meaning; the difference is position and register. 'No longer' goes mid-sentence and suits writing; 'not... any longer' splits around the verb and suits speech.
minimal_pair: He doesn't work here any longer.

confusables.difference: Interchangeable in speech. 'Any longer' is very slightly more formal than 'any more'.

entry_json.avoid: Keep the two parts apart: the negative goes with the verb and 'any longer' goes at the end. Not 'I not any longer go'.

entry_json.definition: used to answer 'no' emphatically, or to reply politely to thanks; also used after a negative verb to strengthen it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: 'Was the exam stressful?' 'Not at all, I'd practised enough to feel calm.'
example_sentences: 'Thanks for helping me move.' 'Not at all, it was no trouble.'
I did not enjoy the film at all.
collocations: not at all happy about sth

contexts.text: 'Was the exam stressful?' 'Not at all, I'd practised enough to feel calm.'
'Thanks for helping me move.' 'Not at all, it was no trouble.'
The results were not at all consistent across the three trials.

confusables.difference: Both answer thanks. 'Not at all' is more formal and British; 'you're welcome' is neutral and international.
'No problem' is casual and common with friends; 'not at all' is the polite version for a stranger or a colleague.

entry_json.avoid: When it strengthens a negative it splits: 'I didn't like it at all', not 'I didn't at all like it'.

entry_json.definition: used to add the most surprising item to a negative statement; it stands directly in front of the word it emphasises
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Nobody in the class had heard of the writer, not even the teacher.
example_sentences: He didn't apologise, not even after the mistake cost the team a week.
The village has no shop, not even a post office.

contexts.text: Nobody in the class had heard of the writer, not even the teacher.
The village has no shop, not even a post office.
Not even the highest earners saw their income rise in real terms.

confusables.difference: 'Even not' is not English word order. The negative comes first: 'not even'.
In a positive sentence 'even' alone does the job: 'Even the teacher had heard of him.' Add 'not' only when the sentence is negative.

entry_json.avoid: Put 'not even' immediately before the surprising word. 'Not even he came' and 'He didn't even come' say different things.

entry_json.definition: used to say that something may be true but does not have to be; a hedge that answers an over-general claim
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A longer essay is not necessarily a better one.
example_sentences: Working from home does not necessarily mean working fewer hours.
'So the cheaper option is worse?' 'Not necessarily.'

contexts.text: A longer essay is not necessarily a better one.
'So a bigger city is always better for jobs?' 'Not necessarily.'
A correlation does not necessarily indicate a causal relationship.

confusables.difference: 'Not always' talks about frequency: it is sometimes untrue. 'Not necessarily' talks about logic: it does not have to follow.
minimal_pair: Cheap flights are not always uncomfortable.
A cheap flight is not necessarily an uncomfortable one.

confusables.difference: The word is almost never used positively on its own. It lives in the negative.

entry_json.avoid: Keep the negative on the auxiliary: 'does not necessarily mean', not 'necessarily does not mean', which reverses the sense.

entry_json.definition: used before the first of two things to signal that a second, larger one is coming; when it opens a sentence the subject and auxiliary swap places
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Not only does the scheme reduce traffic, it also raises money for the buses.
example_sentences: The city is not only crowded but expensive.
Not only did the temperature rise, but rainfall also became less predictable.

contexts.text: Not only does the scheme reduce traffic, it also raises money for the buses.
The city is not only crowded but expensive.
Not only did emissions fall, but energy output rose over the same period.

confusables.difference: Not a phrase in English. The order is fixed: 'not only'.
'As well as' simply adds; 'not only' also signals that what follows is the stronger point.
minimal_pair: As well as reducing traffic, it raises money.
Not only does it reduce traffic, it raises money.

entry_json.avoid: If you start a sentence with 'Not only', you must invert: 'Not only does it cost more', never 'Not only it costs more'.

entry_json.definition: a paired linker joining two items of the same kind; whatever follows 'not only' and 'but also' must be the same grammatical type, two nouns, two verbs or two clauses
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cycling is not only cheaper but also faster than driving across the centre at rush hour.
example_sentences: The course improved not only my vocabulary but also my confidence in speaking.
Not only did the factory close, but also the two firms that supplied it.

contexts.text: Cycling is not only cheaper but also faster than driving across the centre at rush hour.
The course improved not only my vocabulary but also my confidence.
The policy affected not only urban households but also rural ones.

confusables.difference: 'Both... and' just joins two equal items. 'Not only... but also' adds emphasis and builds to the second one.
minimal_pair: It is both cheaper and faster.
It is not only cheaper but also faster.

confusables.difference: Wrong pairing. 'Not only' takes 'but also', never 'and also'.

entry_json.avoid: Keep both halves parallel. Not 'not only cheaper but also it is faster'; write 'not only cheaper but also faster'.

entry_json.definition: used to add one more item that strengthens the point you have just made; it takes a noun or a noun phrase after it, not a full clause
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Living in the centre means high rent, not to mention the noise.
example_sentences: The trip involved two flights and a long coach journey, not to mention the cost.
Fast food is high in salt and fat, not to mention sugar.
collocations: not to mention the fact that...

contexts.text: Living in the centre means high rent, not to mention the noise.
Cars take up space and produce emissions, not to mention the cost of maintaining roads.
The scheme requires new hardware, not to mention staff training.

confusables.difference: 'Let alone' follows a negative and says the second thing is even less likely: 'He can't cook rice, let alone a whole meal.' 'Not to mention' simply adds weight to a positive list.
minimal_pair: I can't afford the rent, let alone the bills.
The rent is high, not to mention the bills.

confusables.difference: 'Besides' introduces an extra argument and can start a sentence; 'not to mention' attaches an extra item to the sentence you are already in.

entry_json.avoid: Do not follow it with a finite clause. Write 'not to mention the cost' or 'not to mention the fact that it is costly', never 'not to mention it is costly'.

entry_json.definition: only, and nothing else; it goes before a noun or a bare verb and carries a note of criticism or of surprise at how little there is
entry_json.own_context_sentence: For the first week the town centre was nothing but building sites and closed shops.
example_sentences: He has done nothing but complain since the timetable changed.
The desert road offers nothing but sand for two hundred kilometres.

contexts.text: For the first week the town centre was nothing but building sites and closed shops.
He's done nothing but complain since the timetable changed.
The early results showed nothing but random variation.

confusables.difference: Almost opposite. 'Nothing but X' means only X; 'anything but X' means definitely not X.
minimal_pair: The meal was nothing but rice.
The meal was anything but cheap.

confusables.difference: 'Only' is neutral. 'Nothing but' adds the feeling that this is too little, or too much of one thing.

entry_json.avoid: After 'do nothing but' use the bare infinitive: 'does nothing but complain', not 'does nothing but complaining'.

entry_json.definition: not at all similar to something, or, before an amount, far less than it; the meaning changes with what follows
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The recording in the test was nothing like the practice material I had used.
example_sentences: The photograph looked nothing like the hotel we actually stayed in.
They raised nothing like the amount they had hoped for.

contexts.text: The recording in the test was nothing like the practice material I had used.
They raised nothing like the amount they had hoped for.

confusables.difference: Before a noun it means dissimilar; before a number or 'enough' it means far short of it. Context decides.
A separate, positive idiom meaning nothing is better: 'There's nothing like a cold drink after a run.' Note the 'there is'.
minimal_pair: There's nothing like a good coffee.

entry_json.avoid: Mostly spoken. In Task 2 prefer 'bears little resemblance to' or 'falls well short of'.

entry_json.definition: used to say that something is obvious or expected, or to agree readily to a request; it can open a sentence, sit mid-sentence between commas, or stand alone
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Of course, not every student learns at the same speed.
example_sentences: 'Could I borrow your notes?' 'Of course, take them for the weekend.'
The city has grown quickly and, of course, house prices have risen with it.

contexts.text: Of course, not every student learns at the same speed.
'Could I borrow your notes?' 'Of course, take them for the weekend.'
Of course, these figures cover only the three largest cities.

confusables.difference: Both mark something as expected. 'Naturally' is slightly more formal; 'of course' can sound impatient if you use it about something the listener did not know.
As an answer, 'certainly' is more formal and more distant. 'Of course' is warm and friendly.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it about a fact your reader could not be expected to know; it implies they should already have known, and can read as rude.

entry_json.definition: someone you have been friends with for a long time; 'old' describes the friendship, not the person's age
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I met an old friend from primary school at the station last week.
example_sentences: She is staying with an old friend while she looks for a flat.
We are old friends, so we can go months without speaking and pick up where we left off.

contexts.text: I met an old friend from primary school at the station last week.
She is staying with an old friend while she looks for a flat.

confusables.difference: 'Old friend' means a long friendship. If you mean the person is elderly, say 'a friend who is in her eighties'.
'Close' is about how strong the friendship is; 'old' is about how long it has lasted. They do not always go together.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'an old friend of mine', not 'a my old friend'. English does not allow an article and a possessive together.

entry_json.definition: on that particular day; days of the week take 'on', and the day is always capitalised
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have my speaking test on Monday morning at nine.
example_sentences: The library is closed on Monday for maintenance.
We usually have the team meeting on Monday.

contexts.text: I have my speaking test on Monday morning at nine.
The library is closed on Monday for maintenance.

confusables.difference: The plural means every Monday, as a habit. The singular means one particular Monday.
Never 'in' with a day. Use 'in' for months and years, 'on' for days and dates, 'at' for clock times.

entry_json.avoid: Do not lowercase the day. Monday, Tuesday and the rest are always capitals in English, even mid-sentence.

entry_json.definition: broadcast by television; there is no article before TV in this phrase
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I saw a documentary about the Amazon on TV last night.
example_sentences: The match is on TV at eight, so nobody wants to go out.
Adverts on TV still reach more people over sixty than online ones do.

contexts.text: I saw a documentary about the Amazon on TV last night.
Adverts on TV still reach more people over sixty than online ones do.

confusables.difference: 'On TV' means broadcast. 'On the TV' can mean physically on top of the television set: 'The remote is on the TV.'
minimal_pair: The remote is on the TV.

confusables.difference: Never 'in TV' for a programme. 'In television' only works about the industry: 'She works in television.'

entry_json.avoid: Do not add 'the' when you mean broadcast: 'I saw it on TV', not 'on the TV'.

entry_json.definition: a dictionary label showing that the pattern 'on + day of the week' works for every day, not only Tuesday; the entry to learn is 'on + Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday...'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The pattern is fixed: on Tuesday, on Wednesday, on Thursday, and so on for every day of the week.
example_sentences: The gym is busiest on Tuesday and Thursday evenings.
Deliveries arrive on Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday.

contexts.text: The gym is busiest on Tuesday and Thursday evenings.
Deliveries arrive on Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday.

confusables.difference: Days never take 'at'. Use 'on' for days, 'at' for clock times and 'at the weekend'.
The 'etc.' here belongs to the dictionary, not to your sentence. Never write 'I'll come on Tuesday, etc.'

entry_json.avoid: Do not copy 'etc.' into your own sentence. It is the list's shorthand for 'and the other days', not part of the English phrase.

entry_json.definition: regularly, at repeated intervals; a formal alternative to the adverb, usually placed at the end of the clause
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Employees who exercise on a regular basis take fewer days of sick leave.
example_sentences: The equipment is inspected on a regular basis to meet safety rules.
Families who eat together on a regular basis report stronger relationships.

contexts.text: Employees who exercise on a regular basis take fewer days of sick leave.
I go to the pool on a regular basis, usually twice a week.
Air quality is measured on a regular basis at twelve city sites.

confusables.difference: Same meaning in four extra words. Examiners reward range, but 'regularly' is often the better choice; keep the long form for variety, not for every sentence.
minimal_pair: He exercises on a regular basis.

confusables.difference: Wrong preposition pattern. It is 'on a ... basis', with the adjective in the middle.

entry_json.avoid: Do not overuse it to pad a sentence. Two uses of 'on a ... basis' in one essay is plenty.

entry_json.definition: acting for someone else, or speaking as their representative; the person represented follows 'of', and it never splits
entry_json.own_context_sentence: On behalf of the whole department, I would like to thank the volunteers.
example_sentences: The lawyer signed the contract on behalf of her client.
Charities campaign on behalf of people who have no other voice.

contexts.text: On behalf of the whole department, I would like to thank the volunteers.
The lawyer signed the contract on behalf of her client.
Charities campaign on behalf of groups that governments overlook.

confusables.difference: When the person is a pronoun, the possessive form is used and 'of' disappears: 'on my behalf', 'on their behalf', never 'on behalf of me'.
minimal_pair: He spoke on behalf of me.

confusables.difference: American usage sometimes allows 'in behalf of' for 'for the benefit of'. In British English, and in IELTS, use 'on behalf of'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it to mean 'because of'. It means 'as the representative of' or 'for the benefit of', not 'as a result of'.

entry_json.definition: on or onto a ship, plane, train or bus; also, in a figurative sense, part of a team or agreeing with a plan
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There were four hundred passengers on board when the ferry left the harbour.
example_sentences: Please switch your phone to flight mode once you are on board.
The scheme will only work if the local councils are on board.

contexts.text: There were four hundred passengers on board when the ferry left the harbour.
Please switch your phone to flight mode once you are on board.
The reform will only succeed if employers are brought on board early.

confusables.difference: One word, slightly more formal, and it can take an object directly: 'aboard the ship'. 'On board' usually stands alone or takes 'of' rarely.
Written as one word it is an adjective before a noun: 'onboard entertainment'. Two words after the verb: 'the food served on board'.

entry_json.avoid: The figurative sense, 'get everyone on board', is business-speak. It is fine in Speaking Part 3 but sounds loose in Task 2.

entry_json.definition: affecting or involving each of the two groups, or physically on each side of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There were casualties on both sides of the dispute before the talks began.
example_sentences: Trees have been planted on both sides of the new road.
The argument has reasonable people on both sides.
collocations: on both sides of the road
on both sides of the argument

contexts.text: Trees have been planted on both sides of the new road.
There are strong arguments on both sides of this debate.
There are shops on both sides of the street where I grew up.

confusables.difference: 'Either side' means one and the other taken separately, and is common with a singular noun after it: 'a chair on either side of the desk'. 'Both sides' takes a plural.
minimal_pair: on both sides of the door
on either side of the door

confusables.difference: Wrong preposition. Sides take 'on'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not follow it with a plural noun after 'of': write 'on both sides of the road', not 'of the roads', when there is one road.

entry_json.definition: placed straight after a question word to show surprise, confusion or annoyance; also literally, meaning on this planet
entry_json.own_context_sentence: How on earth did they build the bridge in eleven months?
example_sentences: What on earth made you take a night flight before an exam?
It is the largest living structure on earth.

contexts.text: How on earth did they build the bridge in eleven months?
The reef is the largest living structure on earth.

confusables.difference: 'On earth' after a question word is emotional; 'in the world' after a superlative is neutral: 'the tallest building in the world'.
minimal_pair: Why on earth did he leave?
It is the tallest building in the world.

confusables.difference: With 'the' it is literal soil or ground: 'seeds lying on the earth'. Without 'the' it means the planet.

entry_json.avoid: The emphatic use is spoken only. Never write 'Why on earth do governments allow this?' in Task 2.

entry_json.definition: away from home for a period of rest or travel; there is no article before 'holiday' in this phrase
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We were on holiday in the north of Spain when the photograph was taken.
example_sentences: She is on holiday until the ninth, so her replacement will answer emails.
Most people go on holiday in July or August, which is why prices peak then.

contexts.text: We were on holiday in the north of Spain when the photograph was taken.
Most families go on holiday during the school break, so fares rise sharply.

confusables.difference: 'On holiday' is British; 'on vacation' is American. IELTS accepts both, but keep one variety across the whole answer.
Never 'in holiday'. The preposition is 'on'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not add an article: 'on holiday', not 'on the holiday' or 'on a holiday', unless you name a specific one.

entry_json.definition: alone, or without help from anybody; it goes at the end of the clause and the possessive must match the subject
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I moved to the city on my own at eighteen and knew nobody there.
example_sentences: I prefer studying on my own because I lose concentration in groups.
I managed to assemble the whole desk on my own.

contexts.text: I moved to the city on my own at eighteen and knew nobody there.
I prefer studying on my own because I lose concentration in groups.

confusables.difference: Almost identical. 'By myself' leans towards physically alone; 'on my own' leans towards unaided. In everyday speech either works.
Not English. It is 'on my own', with 'own', or 'by myself', with the reflexive.

entry_json.avoid: Match the possessive to the subject: 'she did it on her own', never 'she did it on my own' unless you really mean you.

entry_json.definition: broadcast by television; the full word takes no article in this phrase, exactly like 'on TV'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The debate was shown live on television and watched by four million people.
example_sentences: Advertising on television is still the most expensive way to reach a mass audience.
She first appeared on television as a weather presenter.

contexts.text: The debate was shown live on television and watched by four million people.
Advertising on television reaches older audiences more reliably than social media does.

confusables.difference: Identical meaning. 'On TV' suits speech and informal writing; 'on television' suits Task 1 and Task 2.
Adding 'the' points at the physical set rather than the medium.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'in television' for a programme. 'In television' means working in the industry.

entry_json.definition: using something as the reason or the evidence for a decision; a noun or a gerund follows 'of', never a full clause
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Applicants are selected on the basis of experience rather than qualifications alone.
example_sentences: The conclusion was reached on the basis of only two interviews.
Loans are granted on the basis of what the household earns.

contexts.text: Applicants are selected on the basis of experience rather than qualifications alone.
The conclusion was reached on the basis of only two interviews.
They chose the flat on the basis of the commute, not the rent.

confusables.difference: 'On the grounds that' takes a clause and gives a justification; 'on the basis of' takes a noun and gives the evidence used.
minimal_pair: It was rejected on the grounds that it was too costly.
It was rejected on the basis of cost.

confusables.difference: 'Based on' is the participle version and is more common in speech: 'a decision based on cost'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not follow it with a clause: write 'on the basis of the results', not 'on the basis of the results were poor'.

entry_json.definition: on the strip of sand or stones beside the sea; 'on' is used because the beach is treated as a surface
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We spent most of the afternoon on the beach and swam before dinner.
example_sentences: Litter left on the beach ends up in the sea within days.
There is a small cafe at the far end of the beach.

contexts.text: We spent most of the afternoon on the beach and swam before dinner.
Litter left on the beach ends up in the sea within days.

confusables.difference: 'At the beach' names the place you went to; 'on the beach' puts you on the sand itself. Both are correct English.
minimal_pair: We were at the beach all day.
The children were playing on the beach.

confusables.difference: Never 'in the beach'. You can be in the sea, but on the beach.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse 'beach', the sand, with 'coast', the whole shoreline of a country.

entry_json.definition: resting on the surface you walk on inside a building; also used for a level of a building, as in 'on the third floor'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There was no space left, so I sat on the floor at the back of the lecture hall.
example_sentences: He left his bag on the floor and somebody nearly tripped over it.
Our flat is on the fourth floor and there is no lift.

contexts.text: There was no space left, so I sat on the floor at the back of the lecture hall.
Our flat is on the fourth floor and there is no lift.

confusables.difference: 'Floor' is indoors; 'ground' is outdoors. A book falls on the floor at home and on the ground in the park.
minimal_pair: The keys were on the floor of the car.
The keys were on the ground outside.

confusables.difference: Only for something set into it: 'a hatch in the floor'. Anything resting on top is 'on the floor'.

entry_json.avoid: British English calls the entrance level the ground floor, so 'the first floor' is one storey up. Be careful when describing a building in Task 1.

entry_json.definition: on the surface of the earth outdoors; also used figuratively for the real situation in a place, as opposed to plans made elsewhere
entry_json.own_context_sentence: After the storm there were branches lying on the ground across the whole park.
example_sentences: Snow stayed on the ground for almost a fortnight.
Reports from officials on the ground contradicted the government's figures.

contexts.text: After the storm there were branches lying on the ground across the whole park.
Reports from staff on the ground contradicted the official figures.

confusables.difference: Outdoors is ground, indoors is floor.
A different phrase entirely: 'on the grounds of cost' means for that reason. Note the plural and the 'of'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'on the ground' for an indoor surface; British readers will find it odd.

entry_json.definition: available through, or done using, the internet; British usage keeps 'the' before 'internet' in this phrase
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Most of my research for the presentation was done on the internet in a single evening.
example_sentences: Anything published on the internet is very difficult to remove afterwards.
I found the recipe on the internet rather than in a cookbook.
collocations: look sth up on the internet

contexts.text: Most of my research for the presentation was done on the internet in a single evening.
Anything published on the internet is very difficult to remove afterwards.

confusables.difference: 'Online' is one word and works as adjective or adverb: 'I booked online', 'online shopping'. 'On the internet' is longer and slightly more old-fashioned.
minimal_pair: I bought it on the internet.

confusables.difference: Wrong preposition. English uses 'on the internet'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop the article in British English: 'on the internet', not 'on internet'.

entry_json.definition: on the left-hand side; useful in Task 1 for pointing at part of a map, plan or chart
entry_json.own_context_sentence: On the left of the map there is a car park, and the school stands opposite it.
example_sentences: The post office is on the left, just past the traffic lights.
The column on the left shows figures for 1990.

contexts.text: On the left of the map there is a car park, and the school stands opposite it.
The post office is on the left, just past the traffic lights.

confusables.difference: 'On the left' names a position; 'to the left' names a direction of movement or a relative position: 'turn to the left', 'to the left of the door'.
minimal_pair: The bank is on the left.
Turn to the left at the lights.

confusables.difference: Wrong. Sides take 'on' or 'to'.

entry_json.avoid: In Task 1 map questions, say what is on the left of what: 'on the left of the site', not just 'on the left', which leaves the examiner guessing.

entry_json.definition: used to introduce the first of two contrasting views; it commits you to writing 'on the other hand' afterwards
entry_json.own_context_sentence: On the one hand, tourism brings income to remote regions; on the other, it drives up local house prices.
example_sentences: On the one hand the technology saves time, and on the other it removes jobs.
On the one hand, remote work reduces commuting; on the other hand, it isolates new staff.
collocations: on the one hand... on the other hand

contexts.text: On the one hand, tourism brings income to remote regions; on the other, it drives up local house prices.
On the one hand the technology saves time, and on the other it removes jobs.

confusables.difference: 'On the other hand' can appear alone to introduce a contrast. 'On the one hand' cannot; it must be answered.
minimal_pair: On the other hand, costs are rising.
On the one hand costs are rising; on the other, wages are too.

confusables.difference: 'In one hand' is literal, about holding something. The linker is 'on the one hand'.

entry_json.avoid: Never leave it unanswered. If you write 'On the one hand' and no contrast follows, the paragraph reads as unfinished.

entry_json.definition: used to introduce a contrasting point; it can follow 'on the one hand' or stand alone, and it normally opens a sentence with a comma after it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cars are convenient. On the other hand, they are the main source of the city's air pollution.
example_sentences: Living at home saves money. On the other hand, it can delay independence.
The course is expensive; on the other hand, it guarantees a work placement.

contexts.text: Cars are convenient. On the other hand, they are the main source of the city's air pollution.
I like living in the centre. On the other hand, the rent is enormous.
On the other hand, spending on rail fell steadily over the same period.

confusables.difference: A very common slip. It is 'on the other hand'; 'in the other hand' means holding something in your other hand.
minimal_pair: On the other hand, it is expensive.
She held the cup in the other hand.

confusables.difference: Both mark contrast. 'However' is lighter and can move around the sentence; 'on the other hand' is heavier and signals two balanced sides.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it simply to add another point in the same direction. It must mark a genuine contrast, or the reader is misled.

entry_json.definition: on the opposite side of something already mentioned; used alone when the thing is clear from context
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The station is on the other side, so you will need to use the footbridge.
example_sentences: There are flats along one bank and offices on the other side.
The market is on this side of the river and the cathedral is on the other side.
collocations: on the other side of the road

contexts.text: The station is on the other side, so you will need to use the footbridge.
Housing lines one bank of the river, while industry occupies the other side.

confusables.term: on the other side of sth
confusables.difference: Add 'of' plus a noun when the reference is not obvious: 'on the other side of the road'.
minimal_pair: It's on the other side of the road.

confusables.difference: Wrong preposition; sides take 'on'.

entry_json.avoid: In Task 1 do not leave it bare. Name what it is the other side of, or the description becomes unclear.

vocab_new.lemma: on the other side of sth

entry_json.headword: on the other side of sth
entry_json.definition: on the opposite side of a named thing; the noun follows 'of' and the phrase does not split
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The new hospital was built on the other side of the motorway, which cut the journey for half the county.
example_sentences: My grandparents live on the other side of the country.
There is a small park on the other side of the railway line.
collocations: on the other side of the road
on the other side of the river
on the other side of town

chunk.pattern: on the other side of sth

contexts.text: The new hospital was built on the other side of the motorway.
My grandparents live on the other side of the country, so I only see them twice a year.

confusables.difference: 'Across the road' is shorter and more natural in speech; 'on the other side of the road' is more precise about position rather than movement.
minimal_pair: He lives on the other side of the road.

confusables.term: in the other side of sth
confusables.difference: Wrong preposition. Always 'on'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop 'of' before the noun. 'On the other side the river' is ungrammatical.

entry_json.definition: done or felt by that person or group; a formal way of naming who is responsible for an attitude or an action, and it follows the noun it explains
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The delay was the result of poor planning on the part of the contractor.
example_sentences: There was little enthusiasm for the scheme on the part of local residents.
The report identifies a failure on the part of the regulator.
collocations: a failure on the part of sb
reluctance on the part of sb

contexts.text: The delay was the result of poor planning on the part of the contractor.
There was little enthusiasm for the scheme on the part of local residents.

confusables.difference: With a pronoun, use the possessive and drop 'of': 'on their part', 'on my part', not 'on the part of them'.
minimal_pair: a mistake on the part of them

confusables.difference: 'For their part' means 'as far as they are concerned' and introduces their side of an argument. Different job.
minimal_pair: Poor planning on their part caused it.
For their part, residents blamed the council.

entry_json.avoid: This is formal written English. In Speaking it sounds stiff; say 'the contractor planned it badly' instead.

entry_json.definition: using the telephone, or connected to somebody by telephone; the article is kept, and it usually follows 'be' or a verb of talking
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She was on the phone to the bank for nearly forty minutes.
example_sentences: I spend far more time on the phone now that half the team works remotely.
Sorry, he is on the phone at the moment; can I take a message?

contexts.text: She was on the phone to the bank for nearly forty minutes.
Staff now spend more time on the phone than in face-to-face meetings.

confusables.difference: 'By phone' describes the method of contact: 'Bookings can be made by phone.' 'On the phone' describes somebody in the middle of a call.
Wrong preposition. It is 'on the phone'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop the article. 'On phone' is not English; say 'on the phone'.

entry_json.definition: on the right-hand side; the mirror image of 'on the left' and equally useful for describing maps and plans
entry_json.own_context_sentence: On the right of the diagram there is a second entrance, added after 2005.
example_sentences: The library is on the right, opposite the sports hall.
The bar on the right of the chart represents the final year.

contexts.text: On the right of the diagram there is a second entrance, added after 2005.
The library is on the right, opposite the sports hall.

confusables.difference: 'On the right' is position; 'to the right' is direction or relative placement: 'turn to the right'.
minimal_pair: The shop is on the right.
Turn to the right after the bridge.

confusables.difference: 'In the right' is a separate idiom meaning morally correct: 'She was in the right.'

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'in the right side'. It is 'on the right' or 'on the right-hand side'.

entry_json.definition: outside in a particular street; British English often prefers 'in the street' for this literal sense, while 'on the street' is standard in American English and in fixed expressions
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I bumped into an old colleague on the street outside the station.
example_sentences: Parking on the street is free after six in the evening.
The protest filled the street in front of the town hall.

contexts.text: Parking on the street is free after six in the evening.
I bumped into an old colleague on the street outside the station.

confusables.difference: British English says 'I met her in the street'; American English says 'on the street'. Both are understood, but stay consistent.
minimal_pair: I met her in the street.
I met her on the street.

confusables.difference: The plural, without an article before a noun, usually means homeless or in public disorder. Very different meaning.

entry_json.avoid: Do not mix varieties inside one answer. Choose British 'in the street' or American 'on the street' and keep to it.

entry_json.definition: living without a home, or out in public in large numbers; the plural changes the meaning from a literal location to a social one
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Thousands of people are sleeping on the streets in cities that have no shortage of empty buildings.
example_sentences: When the factory closed, hundreds of workers were left on the streets.
Police were on the streets throughout the weekend of the festival.

contexts.text: Thousands of people are sleeping on the streets in cities that have no shortage of empty buildings.
Police were on the streets throughout the weekend of the festival.

confusables.difference: The singular is literal position. The plural is about homelessness or crowds in public.
minimal_pair: He ended up on the streets.

confusables.difference: 'Homeless' is the neutral adjective and is safer in Task 2; 'on the streets' is vivid but narrower, since many homeless people are in hostels.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it for one person standing outside. For that, say 'in the street'.

entry_json.definition: broadcast, in informal British speech, where the article is often kept; with a physical meaning it points at the top of the set itself
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There's a documentary about the coast on the television tonight.
example_sentences: The remote control was on the television, not on the sofa.
My grandparents still say they saw it on the television rather than online.

contexts.text: There's a documentary about the coast on the television tonight.
The remote control was on the television, not on the sofa.

confusables.difference: Without 'the' it is the standard broadcasting phrase and the right choice in writing.
minimal_pair: The match was shown on television.
The match is on the television.

confusables.difference: The same informal spoken pattern with the abbreviation.

entry_json.avoid: In Task 1 or Task 2 drop the article: write 'on television'. The version with 'the' reads as conversational.

entry_json.definition: attached to or hanging against a wall; use 'on', not 'in', because the wall is a surface
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is a large map of the region on the wall behind the reception desk.
example_sentences: The photographs on the wall of the cafe were all taken locally.
We hung a whiteboard on the wall so everyone could see the schedule.

contexts.text: There is a large map of the region on the wall behind the reception desk.
The photographs on the wall of the cafe were all taken locally.

confusables.difference: 'In the wall' means inside it: 'a safe in the wall', 'a crack in the wall'. Anything hanging is 'on the wall'.
Not used for position of objects. 'At the wall' suggests standing next to it.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'in the wall' for a picture or a poster; it changes the meaning to something embedded in the brickwork.

entry_json.definition: during a journey, or approaching and due to arrive soon; often followed by 'to' plus a destination
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I usually listen to a podcast on the way to work.
example_sentences: We stopped for petrol on the way and still arrived early.
The parcel is on the way and should reach you by Friday.

contexts.text: I usually listen to a podcast on the way to work.
The parcel is on the way and should reach you by Friday.

confusables.difference: Completely different. 'In the way' means blocking something: 'Your bag is in the way.'
minimal_pair: I bought it on the way home.
Your bag is in the way.

confusables.difference: 'By the way' changes the subject in conversation. Nothing to do with journeys.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse it with 'in the way'. One preposition changes helpful into obstructive.

entry_json.definition: alone, or without help; the same pattern as 'on my own', with the possessive matching the subject, and it can also mean 'without anything else' about things
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Many older people live on their own and see nobody for days at a time.
example_sentences: Children learn faster when they are allowed to solve some problems on their own.
Subsidies on their own will not persuade people to give up cars.

contexts.text: Many older people live on their own and see nobody for days at a time.
Subsidies on their own will not persuade people to give up their cars.
My cousins travelled around Europe on their own last summer.

confusables.difference: Near-identical. 'By themselves' stresses being physically alone; 'on their own' stresses unaided.
minimal_pair: They fixed it on their own.

confusables.difference: 'Alone' is a single adjective and can sound literary or sad. 'On their own' is the neutral everyday choice.

entry_json.avoid: Keep the possessive in agreement: 'the company on its own', not 'the company on their own', if you treat the company as singular.

entry_json.definition: at the arranged time, neither early nor late; there is no article, and it usually follows the verb
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Only sixty per cent of trains on that line arrive on time.
example_sentences: Please submit the assignment on time, as late work loses marks.
The flight left on time despite the weather.

contexts.text: Only sixty per cent of trains on that line arrive on time.
Please submit the assignment on time, as late work loses marks.
I always leave early because I hate not being on time.

confusables.difference: 'On time' means punctual, at the scheduled moment. 'In time' means early enough for something to happen.
minimal_pair: We arrived in time to catch it.

confusables.difference: The formal written equivalent, common in reports. 'On time' is fine in both speech and writing.

entry_json.avoid: Do not add an article: 'on time', never 'on the time'.

entry_json.definition: resting on the highest surface of something; also, figuratively, in addition to something, or in full control of a task
entry_json.own_context_sentence: On top of the rent, we pay nearly two hundred pounds a month in bills.
example_sentences: The files were stacked on top of the cabinet.
She stays on top of her workload by planning each week on a Sunday evening.

contexts.text: On top of the rent, we pay nearly two hundred pounds a month in bills.
The files were stacked on top of the cabinet.
On top of rising fees, students now face higher living costs.

confusables.difference: The formal written equivalent of the figurative sense. Use it in Task 2 where 'on top of' would sound casual.
minimal_pair: On top of the fees, there is rent.
In addition to the fees, there is rent.

confusables.difference: 'Above' means higher than, with a gap. 'On top of' means touching the upper surface.
minimal_pair: The lamp is above the table.
The book is on top of the table.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop 'of'. It is 'on top of the cupboard', never 'on top the cupboard'.

entry_json.definition: alone or unaided, when addressing somebody or speaking about people in general; the possessive changes with the subject
entry_json.own_context_sentence: You will be on your own for the second half of the task, so read the instructions carefully.
example_sentences: Did you build the website on your own, or did somebody help?
Learning a language on your own is possible but slow.

contexts.text: Did you build the website on your own, or did somebody help?
Learning a language on your own is possible but slow.

confusables.difference: Same phrase, different person. Match the possessive to whoever is doing the action.
minimal_pair: I did it on my own.
You did it on your own.

confusables.difference: A separate business phrase meaning self-employed or at your own risk.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'on your self'. The two correct forms are 'on your own' and 'by yourself'.

entry_json.definition: one time in each month; the pattern is 'once + a + period', and 'a' here means 'per'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I go back to my home town about once a month to see my parents.
example_sentences: The committee meets once a month to review spending.
Fire alarms are tested once a month in every building on campus.

contexts.text: I go back to my home town about once a month to see my parents.
The committee meets once a month to review spending.

confusables.difference: Not standard English for frequency. The 'a' already carries the meaning 'per'.
One word, more formal, and it can be an adjective too: 'a monthly meeting'. Useful for variety in Task 1.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'one time a month'. English uses 'once', 'twice', then 'three times'.

entry_json.definition: one time in each week; a fixed frequency expression that usually sits at the end of the clause
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I play football once a week with people from my old school.
example_sentences: The bins are collected once a week in this part of the city.
Adults should do strength exercises at least twice a week, not once a week.

contexts.text: I play football once a week with people from my old school.
The bins are collected once a week in this part of the city.

confusables.difference: The single-word adjective or adverb, useful before a noun: 'a weekly meeting'. 'Once a week' is the natural spoken form.
'In a week' means after seven days have passed, not a frequency.
minimal_pair: I'll be back in a week.

entry_json.avoid: Do not put it before the verb. Say 'I swim once a week', not 'I once a week swim'.

entry_json.definition: one time in each year; often used for annual events and for habits you rarely repeat
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We take a proper holiday once a year, usually in the spring.
example_sentences: The equipment is serviced once a year by an outside engineer.
The festival is held once a year and attracts about ten thousand visitors.

contexts.text: We take a proper holiday once a year, usually in the spring.
The festival is held once a year and attracts about ten thousand visitors.

confusables.difference: The formal adverb, common in Task 1 reports: 'reviewed annually'. 'Once a year' is plainer.
minimal_pair: It is reviewed once a year.

confusables.difference: Adjective or adverb, slightly less formal than 'annually': 'a yearly check'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'one time in a year'. The set phrase is 'once a year'.

entry_json.definition: one more time, especially when the same thing has happened before; it can open a sentence or follow the verb
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Once again the figures show that private car use is rising faster than public transport.
example_sentences: The team finished bottom of the table once again.
Once again, no single explanation accounts for all the results.

contexts.text: Once again the figures show that private car use is rising faster than public transport.
I missed the deadline once again, which is why I now use a calendar.

confusables.difference: 'Once more' is a neutral repetition, often a request: 'Say it once more.' 'Once again' carries a hint that the repetition is expected or tiring.
This means many times, not one more time.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it in a Task 1 report unless the pattern really does repeat. Overusing it makes an even trend sound dramatic.

entry_json.definition: the frequency frame 'once a' followed by a period of time such as day, week, month, term or year; 'a' means 'per', and 'twice' and 'three times' fit the same slot
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The pattern is fixed: once a day, once a week, once a month, once a year.
example_sentences: The tank is refilled once a day during the summer.
Staff are assessed once a term rather than once a year.

contexts.text: The tank is refilled once a day during the summer.
I check my emails about once an hour, which is probably too often.

confusables.difference: 'Once every three days' is the version for longer or irregular gaps; 'once a' works only with a single period.
Not used for frequency, except in the idiom 'once in a while', which means occasionally.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'an' before a vowel sound: 'once an hour', not 'once a hour'.

entry_json.definition: each of two or more people doing something to the others; a reciprocal pronoun that takes the object position, never the subject
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Students on the course are encouraged to give one another feedback before they submit.
example_sentences: Neighbours in the village still look after one another during bad weather.
The two studies contradict one another on almost every point.

contexts.text: Students on the course are encouraged to give one another feedback before they submit.
Neighbours in the village still look after one another during bad weather.
My flatmates and I cook for one another during the week.

confusables.difference: Almost interchangeable. Some traditional guides keep 'each other' for two and 'one another' for three or more, but modern usage treats them as equal; 'one another' is the more formal-sounding of the two.
minimal_pair: The two of them helped each other.

confusables.difference: 'Themselves' means each person acting on himself or herself. 'One another' means acting on the others.

entry_json.avoid: It cannot be the subject of a verb. Not 'One another helped them'; write 'They helped one another'.

entry_json.definition: at some unspecified time in the future, or on a particular unnamed day in the past; the tense of the verb tells you which meaning it carries
entry_json.own_context_sentence: One day I would like to work abroad, ideally somewhere I already speak the language.
example_sentences: One day last winter the whole network stopped because of ice on the lines.
She hopes to open her own studio one day.

contexts.text: One day I would like to work abroad, ideally somewhere I already speak the language.
One day last winter the whole network stopped because of ice on the lines.

confusables.difference: 'Someday' is only about the future and is written as one word in American English. 'One day' can look forwards or backwards.
'The other day' means recently, a few days ago, and is only about the past.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it in Task 2 for a real prediction. 'One day' is vague; write 'within the next decade' or 'in the long term'.

entry_json.definition: a small number, without saying exactly how many; it is followed by a plural countable noun even though it begins with 'one'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: One or two students asked whether the deadline could move, but most were happy with it.
example_sentences: There are one or two problems with the argument that the writer never addresses.
I made one or two changes to the plan before sending it.

contexts.text: One or two students asked whether the deadline could move, but most were happy with it.
There are one or two problems with the argument that the writer never addresses.

confusables.difference: Both mean a small number. 'A couple of' is more informal and usually means exactly two; 'one or two' is deliberately vague.
'A few' suggests three or more; 'one or two' suggests almost none.

entry_json.avoid: Use a plural noun and a plural verb: 'One or two people were late', not 'was late'.

entry_json.definition: disagreeing strongly with something and wanting to prevent it; it follows 'be' and takes a noun or a gerund after 'to', never a bare infinitive
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Most residents are opposed to building on the last piece of green space in the district.
example_sentences: The union is opposed to any change in working hours without consultation.
She is not opposed to the idea in principle, only to the cost.

contexts.text: Most residents are opposed to building on the last piece of green space in the district.
The union is opposed to any change in working hours without consultation.
I'm not opposed to exams, but I think coursework should count too.

confusables.difference: A different phrase meaning 'rather than', used to contrast two options: 'cycling as opposed to driving'. It expresses no disapproval.
minimal_pair: I am opposed to driving in the centre.
I walk, as opposed to driving.

confusables.difference: 'Against' is shorter and more common in speech: 'I'm against it.' 'Opposed to' is the formal written version.

entry_json.avoid: The 'to' here is a preposition, so use the -ing form: 'opposed to building', never 'opposed to build'.

entry_json.definition: approximately, placed immediately after a number or an amount to show it is a rough figure
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The walk to the station takes ten minutes or so.
example_sentences: There were thirty people or so at the meeting.
We stayed for a week or so before moving on.

contexts.text: The walk to the station takes ten minutes or so.
We stayed for a week or so before moving on.

confusables.difference: 'About' goes before the number, 'or so' after it. Do not use both.
The formal written equivalent, and the right choice for Task 1: 'approximately 40 per cent'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not double the hedge. 'About ten minutes or so' is redundant; choose one.

entry_json.definition: added after a person's name or role to show you are not sure exactly who; a vague-language tag used only in conversation
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It was the receptionist or somebody who signed for the parcel.
example_sentences: Ask your tutor or somebody in the department office.
I think it was her brother or somebody who drove them to the airport.

contexts.text: It was the receptionist or somebody who signed for the parcel.
Ask your tutor or somebody in the department office.

confusables.difference: 'Or somebody' stands in for a person; 'or something' stands in for a thing or an activity.
'Or so' hedges a number, not an identity.

entry_json.avoid: Never write it in Task 1 or Task 2. Vagueness tags cost you marks in writing; name the person or say 'a member of staff'.

entry_json.definition: added after a noun or a phrase to show that you are giving an example rather than the exact thing; a hedge that belongs to relaxed speech
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We could get a coffee or something after the class.
example_sentences: He said he was ill or something, so he missed the presentation.
Bring a jacket or something warm, because the hall gets cold.

contexts.text: We could get a coffee or something after the class.
He said he was ill or something, so he missed the presentation.

confusables.difference: The longer version, slightly softer, and just as informal.
The written equivalent. 'For example' introduces a clear illustration; 'or something' admits you do not know or do not care which.
minimal_pair: a snack, for example a sandwich

entry_json.avoid: Keep it out of writing altogether. In Task 2 it reads as if you could not think of the right word.

entry_json.definition: added after a place to show you are unsure exactly where; the place version of 'or something'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I think the conference is in Manchester or somewhere in the north.
example_sentences: They moved to Canada or somewhere like that a few years ago.
Leave it on the desk or somewhere she will see it.

contexts.text: I think the conference is in Manchester or somewhere in the north.
They moved to Canada or somewhere like that a few years ago.

confusables.difference: 'Or somewhere' hedges a place; 'or something' hedges a thing.
A stronger admission that you have no idea: 'He left it somewhere or other.'

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it in writing. If the location matters, name it; if it does not, leave it out.

entry_json.definition: added after a singular noun to mean a small, unspecified number; the noun before it stays singular
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Give it a day or two and the swelling will go down.
example_sentences: I have a question or two about the reading list.
A mile or two further on, the path joins the river.

contexts.text: Give it a day or two and the swelling will go down.
A mile or two further on, the path joins the river.

confusables.difference: 'One or two' comes before a plural noun; 'a ... or two' wraps around a singular one.
More informal, and usually means exactly two.

entry_json.avoid: Keep the noun singular: 'a day or two', not 'a days or two'.

entry_json.definition: people who are not rich, famous or in positions of power; a common phrase in argument writing for naming the general public
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Policies that look sensible on paper often make life harder for ordinary people.
example_sentences: The scheme was designed by economists rather than by ordinary people who use the buses.
Rising energy prices affect ordinary people far more than large companies.

contexts.text: Policies that look sensible on paper often make life harder for ordinary people.
Rising energy prices affect ordinary people far more than large companies.
Museums should be for ordinary people, not just for specialists.

confusables.difference: 'Normal people' implies that everyone else is abnormal and can sound insulting. 'Ordinary people' is the neutral choice.
More formal and more precise for Task 2; 'ordinary people' carries a slight sympathy with them.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it too often in one essay. Repeated three or four times it starts to sound like a slogan rather than an argument.

entry_json.definition: except for, or apart from; it usually follows a negative statement and takes a noun, a pronoun or a clause
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Other than the cost, there is no serious objection to the proposal.
example_sentences: The building has no purpose other than storage.
Nobody other than the two authors had seen the data.

contexts.text: Other than the cost, there is no serious objection to the proposal.
The building has no purpose other than storage.
Other than swimming, I don't do much exercise.

confusables.difference: 'Rather than' chooses between two options. 'Other than' excludes something from a group.
minimal_pair: I do nothing other than walk.

confusables.difference: Very close in meaning and more common in speech; 'other than' is more formal and prefers a negative context.

entry_json.avoid: It works best after a negative. 'Other than the cost, it is fine' is natural, but 'Other than the cost, everyone likes it' is better as 'apart from'.

entry_json.definition: used to say what is the right thing to do or what is likely to be true; it is a modal, so it keeps 'to' before the verb but takes no 'do' in questions and negatives
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Schools ought to teach basic personal finance before students leave.
example_sentences: You ought to see a doctor if the cough lasts more than three weeks.
The parcel ought to arrive tomorrow if it left the depot last night.

contexts.text: Schools ought to teach basic personal finance before students leave.
You ought to see a doctor if the cough lasts more than three weeks.

confusables.difference: Nearly the same meaning. 'Should' is far more common, especially in questions and negatives; 'ought to' sounds slightly more like a moral duty.
The 'to' is part of the modal and cannot be dropped: 'ought to go', never 'ought go'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not add 'do': it is 'You ought not to go', or more naturally 'You shouldn't go', never 'You don't ought to go'.

entry_json.definition: from inside something to the outside, made from a material, or no longer having any of something; the meaning depends on the noun that follows
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Two out of every five journeys in the city are made on foot.
example_sentences: The bench was made out of recycled plastic.
We ran out of time before the last question.

contexts.text: Two out of every five journeys in the city are made on foot.
The bench was made out of recycled plastic.
I got out of the taxi at the wrong entrance.

confusables.difference: Not a standard pair in English except with 'under': 'out from under'. Use 'out of'.
'Off' leaves a surface, 'out of' leaves an enclosed space: 'off the bus' but 'out of the car'.
minimal_pair: He got out of the car.

entry_json.avoid: For proportions in Task 1, keep the pattern whole: 'three out of ten', never 'three of ten'.

entry_json.definition: in the wider world beyond where you are, especially when talking about what exists or is available; informal, and usually placed after the noun
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There are a lot of free courses out there if you know where to look.
example_sentences: The job market out there is tougher than it looks from inside a university.
Plenty of people out there would take that offer immediately.

contexts.text: There are a lot of free courses out there if you know where to look.
The job market out there is tougher than it looks from inside a university.

confusables.difference: The written equivalent. Task 2 wants 'a wide range of free courses is available', not 'out there'.
'Over there' points at a place you can see. 'Out there' means the world in general.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write it in an essay. It is conversational and adds no information a marker can credit.

entry_json.definition: during the whole of a period of time; it takes a period after 'of', and it suits describing change in a Task 1 report
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Over the course of the decade, car ownership doubled while bus use fell by a third.
example_sentences: Attitudes to recycling changed considerably over the course of a single generation.
Over the course of the trial, three participants withdrew.
collocations: over the course of the year
over the course of a decade

contexts.text: Over the course of the decade, car ownership doubled while bus use fell by a third.
Attitudes to recycling changed considerably over the course of a single generation.

confusables.difference: 'During' is shorter and neutral. 'Over the course of' stresses that the change was gradual and continuous.
minimal_pair: over the course of the decade

confusables.difference: 'In the course of' often means 'while doing something': 'in the course of the investigation'. Very close, slightly less about duration.

entry_json.avoid: Follow it with a period of time, not an event: 'over the course of the year', not 'over the course of the meeting was long'.

entry_json.definition: gradually, during a long period in the past up to now; it works with the present perfect because the period continues
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Over the years the town has changed from a fishing port into a tourist destination.
example_sentences: I have learned over the years that revision works better in short blocks.
Over the years the university has added three new faculties.

contexts.text: Over the years the town has changed from a fishing port into a tourist destination.
I have learned over the years that revision works better in short blocks.

confusables.difference: Singular means within one particular year; plural means across many.
minimal_pair: Over the year, sales rose steadily.
Over the years, the town has grown.

confusables.difference: 'For years' emphasises the length of time; 'over the years' emphasises the gradual change during it.

entry_json.avoid: Pair it with the present perfect, not the past simple, when the period reaches the present: 'has changed', not 'changed'.

entry_json.definition: in or to a place a short distance away that you can point at; used when the listener can see or imagine the spot
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The ticket machines are over there, next to the escalator.
example_sentences: You can leave your bag over there with the others.
The people over there are waiting for the same bus.

contexts.text: The ticket machines are over there, next to the escalator.
You can leave your bag over there with the others.

confusables.difference: 'Over there' points at a visible place; 'out there' means the wider world.
'Over there' adds distance and a gesture. Plain 'there' can mean anywhere already mentioned.

entry_json.avoid: It depends on the listener seeing where you point, so it cannot work in writing. Name the place instead.

entry_json.definition: gradually, as time passes; there is no article, and it usually sits at the end of the clause or after the subject
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Over time, the cost of solar panels has fallen to a fraction of what it was.
example_sentences: Skills learned quickly are also lost quickly over time unless they are used.
The soil becomes less fertile over time if the same crop is grown every year.

contexts.text: Over time, the cost of solar panels has fallen to a fraction of what it was.
The soil becomes less fertile over time if the same crop is grown every year.
My accent has softened over time, mostly without me noticing.

confusables.difference: One word, and completely different: extra hours worked beyond the normal day. 'He works overtime.'
'In time' means early enough for something, not gradually.

entry_json.avoid: Keep it as two words. 'Overtime' as one word will be read as extra paid hours.

entry_json.definition: take part in an activity or event with other people; the preposition is always 'in', and it cannot take a direct object without one
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Fewer than half of the students chose to participate in the exchange programme.
example_sentences: Residents were invited to participate in the consultation on the new bypass.
Only volunteers who had participated in the earlier study were contacted again.

contexts.text: Fewer than half of the students chose to participate in the exchange programme.
Residents were invited to participate in the consultation on the new bypass.
I'd like to participate in more sport, but the pool is too far away.

confusables.difference: The same meaning in ordinary English. Use 'take part' in Speaking and 'participate' in Task 2, where it sounds more academic.
minimal_pair: I took part in the survey.

confusables.difference: 'Attend' means simply being present. 'Participate' means doing something once you are there.

entry_json.avoid: Never drop the preposition. 'Participate the event' is wrong; it must be 'participate in the event'.

entry_json.definition: listen or watch carefully and concentrate on something; there is no article before 'attention'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is hard to pay attention in a two-hour lecture without a break.
example_sentences: Drivers who are using a phone cannot pay attention to the road.
Pay attention to the word limit, because going under it costs marks.

contexts.text: It is hard to pay attention in a two-hour lecture without a break.
Drivers who are using a phone cannot pay attention to the road.

confusables.difference: 'Pay attention' is the fixed everyday phrase. 'Give attention to' exists but sounds formal and slightly bureaucratic.
Add 'to' when you name the thing you are concentrating on.

entry_json.avoid: Do not add an article: 'pay attention', not 'pay the attention' or 'pay an attention'.

entry_json.definition: concentrate on a particular person or thing; the thing you concentrate on follows 'to', and the phrase does not split
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Employers pay more attention to work experience than to the name of the university.
example_sentences: If you pay attention to the question wording, half the traps disappear.
Nobody paid any attention to the warning signs until the flooding started.

contexts.text: Employers pay more attention to work experience than to the name of the university.
If you pay attention to the question wording, half the traps disappear.
