confusables.difference: Wrong preposition. It is always 'to'.
'Notice' is a single moment of seeing. 'Pay attention to' is sustained concentration.

entry_json.avoid: When an adjective is added, it goes between: 'pay close attention to', not 'pay attention closely to'.

entry_json.definition: give money in exchange for something; 'pay for' takes the goods or service, while 'pay' alone takes the amount or the person
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I pay for my own course fees by working at weekends.
example_sentences: Taxpayers ultimately pay for infrastructure that private firms then operate.
Who paid for the meal in the end?

contexts.text: I pay for my own course fees by working at weekends.
Taxpayers ultimately pay for infrastructure that private firms then operate.

confusables.difference: 'Pay the bill' and 'pay £20' take no preposition. 'Pay for the meal' needs 'for' because it names the thing bought.
'Pay the plumber' names the person receiving the money, again with no preposition.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'pay for the bill'. A bill is the amount, so it takes no 'for'.

entry_json.definition: for each hour, used for rates of pay, speed or output; 'per' takes a singular noun with no article
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The minimum wage rose to just over eleven pounds per hour.
example_sentences: The turbines generate around two megawatts per hour in good conditions.
Traffic on the ring road averages forty kilometres per hour at peak times.

contexts.text: The minimum wage rose to just over eleven pounds per hour.
Traffic on the ring road averages forty kilometres per hour at peak times.

confusables.difference: In speech, 'a' does the same job: 'twelve pounds an hour'. 'Per hour' is the written and technical version.
Never plural after 'per'. It is 'per hour', 'per day', 'per person'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'per an hour' or 'per the hour'. 'Per' replaces the article.

entry_json.definition: an act of speaking to somebody by telephone; you make, receive, take or return one, but you do not 'do' one
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I had a long phone call with my supervisor about changing the topic.
example_sentences: She made three phone calls before she found a plumber who could come out.
A short phone call would have prevented the whole misunderstanding.

contexts.text: I had a long phone call with my supervisor about changing the topic.
A short phone call would have prevented the whole misunderstanding.

confusables.difference: Just 'a call' is more natural once the context is clear: 'Give me a call.' 'Phone call' spells it out.
Wrong verb. English says 'make a phone call'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'do a phone call'. The verb is 'make', or 'have' when you focus on the conversation.

entry_json.definition: the set of digits used to call a particular telephone; the first noun works as an adjective and stays singular
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Could you give me your phone number in case the room changes?
example_sentences: Please write your phone number clearly on the form.
I changed my phone number when I moved and forgot to tell half my friends.

contexts.text: Could you give me your phone number in case the room changes?
Please write your phone number clearly on the form.

confusables.difference: 'Phone number' is a compound noun: the number belonging to a phone. 'The number of phones' counts devices.
minimal_pair: The number of phones has risen.

confusables.difference: The full form, more formal and common on printed documents.

entry_json.avoid: Keep the first noun singular: 'phone number', never 'phones number'.

entry_json.definition: lift something from a surface, or collect a person or thing in a vehicle; it is separable, so a pronoun must go in the middle: 'pick it up', never 'pick up it'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My father used to pick me up from school every Wednesday.
example_sentences: Could you pick up some milk on the way home?
She picked up a fair amount of Spanish just by living there.
collocations: pick sb up from the airport

contexts.text: My father used to pick me up from school every Wednesday.
Could you pick up some milk on the way home?
Recycling is picked up fortnightly rather than weekly in most districts.

confusables.difference: 'Collect' is the more formal single word and never splits: 'collect the parcel'. 'Pick up' is the everyday choice.
With a full noun either order works: 'pick up the keys' or 'pick the keys up'. With a pronoun only the split version works.

entry_json.avoid: Never say 'pick up me' or 'pick up it'. Pronouns always sit between the verb and 'up'.

entry_json.definition: make arrangements in advance for something you expect; 'plan for' takes a noun, while 'plan to' takes a verb
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cities that fail to plan for population growth end up building in the wrong places.
example_sentences: We had to plan for the possibility that the flight would be cancelled.
Households are being urged to plan for higher energy bills this winter.

contexts.text: Cities that fail to plan for population growth end up building in the wrong places.
We had to plan for the possibility that the flight would be cancelled.

confusables.difference: 'Plan to' introduces an intention and takes an infinitive: 'We plan to move.' 'Plan for' takes a noun: 'We plan for retirement.'
Informal and close to 'intend': 'I'm planning on staying.' Common in speech, less so in Task 2.

entry_json.avoid: Do not mix the two patterns: 'plan for move' is wrong. Use 'plan to move' or 'plan for the move'.

entry_json.definition: spend time amusing yourself with a toy, a game or another person; also used figuratively for handling an idea without commitment
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Children who play with other children learn to negotiate long before they can explain it.
example_sentences: He spent the afternoon playing with the dog in the garden.
The architects played with several designs before choosing the curved roof.

contexts.text: Children who play with other children learn to negotiate long before they can explain it.
He spent the afternoon playing with the dog in the garden.

confusables.difference: With a game or an instrument there is no preposition: 'play football', 'play the piano'. 'Play with' takes a toy or a person.
In sport, 'play against' names the opponent; 'play with' names your team-mate or companion.
minimal_pair: We played against the city team.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'play with football'. Games take no preposition: 'play football'.

entry_json.definition: a way of thinking about something, or an opinion; 'from' introduces whose view it is, and 'in my point of view' is not English
entry_json.own_context_sentence: From an environmental point of view, the cheapest option is rarely the best one.
example_sentences: I can see the argument from the students' point of view as well as the university's.
The report considers the change from an economic point of view only.
collocations: from an economic point of view

contexts.text: From an environmental point of view, the cheapest option is rarely the best one.
I can see the argument from the students' point of view as well as the university's.

confusables.difference: 'In my opinion' takes 'in'; 'point of view' takes 'from'. Mixing them produces the common error 'in my point of view'.
minimal_pair: From my point of view, it is unfair.
In my point of view, it is unfair.

confusables.difference: A more formal synonym: 'from a legal standpoint'. Useful for variety in Task 2.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'in my point of view' or 'according to my point of view'. The preposition is 'from'.

entry_json.definition: tell somebody a fact they seem not to have noticed, or show them where something is; it is separable and can be followed by 'that' plus a clause
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The report points out that most of the growth came from a single sector.
example_sentences: She pointed out the error before the figures went to print.
It is worth pointing out that the survey covered only city residents.

contexts.text: The report points out that most of the growth came from a single sector.
She pointed out the error before the figures went to print.
He pointed out the building where his grandmother was born.

confusables.difference: 'Mention' is neutral, simply saying something. 'Point out' implies correcting a gap in the listener's knowledge.
minimal_pair: She pointed out that the cost had doubled.

confusables.difference: 'Indicate' fits data: 'The graph indicates a rise.' 'Point out' fits people making a remark.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it for your own opinion. 'Point out' claims the statement is a fact, so 'I would like to point out that this is wrong' sounds combative.

entry_json.definition: introduce a fact you want the reader to notice, using a full clause after 'that'; the 'that' can be dropped in speech but is normally kept in academic writing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The authors point out that the sample contained no one under the age of thirty.
example_sentences: Critics point out that the scheme benefits the districts that already have good transport.
It should be pointed out that these figures exclude part-time workers.
collocations: it should be pointed out that...

contexts.text: The authors point out that the sample contained no one under the age of thirty.
Critics point out that the scheme benefits districts that already have good transport.

confusables.difference: With a noun object the phrase splits around it: 'point the error out'. With a clause it does not: 'point out that the figures are wrong'.
minimal_pair: She pointed out that the figures were wrong.

confusables.difference: 'Argue that' presents a contested claim; 'point out that' presents something the writer treats as established fact.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it to launch your own opinion in Task 2. It signals fact, so save it for evidence, and use 'I would argue that' for a view.

entry_json.definition: show or identify a particular thing to somebody; separable, so a pronoun must sit in the middle: 'point it out', never 'point out it'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The guide pointed the old city wall out to us from the top of the hill.
example_sentences: Somebody should have pointed the mistake out before it was printed.
Could you point it out on the map?

contexts.text: Somebody should have pointed the mistake out before it was printed.
Could you point it out on the map?

confusables.difference: Use the unsplit version with a clause and the split version with a noun or pronoun object.
minimal_pair: Point out that there is an error.

confusables.difference: 'Show' is neutral and usually involves demonstrating. 'Point out' is about drawing attention to something already present.

entry_json.avoid: A pronoun object always goes inside: 'point it out', never 'point out it'.

entry_json.definition: a member of the police force; the neutral term that replaced 'policeman' and 'policewoman' in official use
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A police officer was standing at the entrance directing people away from the road.
example_sentences: The city plans to recruit two hundred more police officers over the next three years.
She has worked as a police officer for eleven years.

contexts.text: The city plans to recruit two hundred more police officers over the next three years.
A police officer was standing at the entrance directing people away from the road.

confusables.difference: Still understood, but 'police officer' is the standard neutral term and the safer choice in an exam.
'Police' is always plural as a group noun: 'The police are investigating', not 'is'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'a police' for one person. One person is 'a police officer'; 'the police' is the whole force and takes a plural verb.

entry_json.definition: the local office of the police, where crimes are reported; used with 'at' for location and 'to' for movement
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I had to go to the police station to report the stolen bicycle.
example_sentences: The nearest police station is open only during the day now.
He was questioned at the police station for several hours.

contexts.text: I had to go to the police station to report the stolen bicycle.
The nearest police station is open only during the day now.

confusables.difference: Not English for the building. The compound is 'police station'.
'At the police station' is the usual phrase for being there on business; 'in' focuses on being physically inside.

entry_json.avoid: Keep 'police' singular in the compound: 'police station', not 'polices station'.

entry_json.definition: a place where you can send letters and parcels and often pay bills; usually written as two words, and capitalised when it names the national organisation
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The village post office closed last year and the nearest one is now six miles away.
example_sentences: I need to go to the post office to send this parcel before five.
Rural post offices often serve as the only shop for miles.

contexts.text: The village post office closed last year and the nearest one is now six miles away.
I need to go to the post office to send this parcel before five.

confusables.difference: Not English. The compound is 'post office'.
British English says 'post' for letters and 'post office' for the building; American English says 'mail'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not join it into one word. 'Postoffice' is not standard spelling.

entry_json.definition: the possibility that something may develop or happen; the preposition is 'for' with a noun, and 'to' with a verb
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rooftop solar has enormous potential for reducing household bills in sunny regions.
example_sentences: The site has considerable potential for redevelopment.
There is real potential for conflict when two departments share a budget.

contexts.text: Rooftop solar has enormous potential for reducing household bills in sunny regions.
The site has considerable potential for redevelopment.

confusables.difference: Use 'to' plus an infinitive when the potential belongs to the subject: 'the potential to grow'. Use 'for' plus a noun or gerund otherwise.
'Possibility of' is about whether something might happen; 'potential for' suggests unused capacity that could be developed.

entry_json.avoid: After 'for' use a noun or an -ing form, never a bare infinitive: 'potential for reducing costs', not 'potential for reduce costs'.

entry_json.definition: willing to do something, especially something demanding; it follows 'be' and takes a to-infinitive, and it is about willingness rather than readiness
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Few people are prepared to give up their car unless the alternative is genuinely faster.
example_sentences: The company said it was prepared to negotiate on pay but not on hours.
I would be prepared to move abroad for the right job.

contexts.text: Few people are prepared to give up their car unless the alternative is genuinely faster.
I would be prepared to move abroad for the right job.

confusables.difference: 'Prepared for' plus a noun means ready in advance: 'prepared for the exam'. 'Prepared to' plus a verb means willing.
minimal_pair: I am prepared for the interview.

confusables.difference: Almost the same. 'Prepared to' hints that the person has thought about the cost and accepts it.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse the two patterns. 'Prepared to the exam' is wrong; write 'prepared for the exam'.

entry_json.definition: quite good, better than average but not excellent; 'pretty' here is an adverb of degree and is informal
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My listening is pretty good, but reading under time pressure still worries me.
example_sentences: The food at the canteen is pretty good for the price.
She's pretty good at explaining difficult ideas simply.

contexts.text: My listening is pretty good, but reading under time pressure still worries me.
The food at the canteen is pretty good for the price.

confusables.difference: Similar level, but British 'quite good' can sound faintly disappointed, while 'pretty good' sounds positive.
'Very good' is a clear compliment; 'pretty good' holds something back.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop either preposition. 'Referred as the lost decade' is wrong; it must be 'referred to as'.

entry_json.definition: considered to be something, in the view of other people; almost always passive, and the description follows 'as'

Historians regard him as a reformer.

entry_json.definition: be connected with something, or understand and sympathise with somebody; the preposition is always 'to'

We're related, though only distantly.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'related with'. It is always 'related to'.

The chapter covers issues relating to water supply in dry regions.

entry_json.definition: closely connected with the subject under discussion, or useful for a particular person; the preposition is 'to'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The examiner is looking for examples that are relevant to the question, not simply interesting.
example_sentences: Only two of the studies were relevant to the age group being examined.
The course content should be relevant to the jobs students actually apply for.

contexts.text: The examiner is looking for examples that are relevant to the question, not simply interesting.
Only two of the studies were relevant to the age group being examined.

confusables.difference: 'Related to' means connected in some way. 'Relevant to' means useful for the matter in hand. A fact can be related but not relevant.
minimal_pair: The data is related to housing.
The data is relevant to our question.

confusables.difference: 'For' is possible when you mean useful to a person, but 'to' is the safer standard choice.

entry_json.avoid: Watch the spelling: relevant, with three e-sounds and no 'a' in the middle. 'Relevent' and 'revelant' are both common misspellings.

entry_json.definition: depend on somebody or something to work or to help you; the preposition is 'on', and it is often followed by an -ing form or 'to' plus a verb
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rural communities rely on a bus service that runs three times a day.
example_sentences: The system relies on users updating their details, which many never do.
You cannot rely on the weather in April.
collocations: rely on sb to do sth

contexts.text: Rural communities rely on a bus service that runs three times a day.
The system relies on users updating their details, which many never do.
I rely on my phone far more than I would like to admit.

confusables.difference: Almost the same. 'Rely on' suggests trust that something will work; 'depend on' can also mean 'be determined by': 'It depends on the weather.'
Wrong preposition. It is always 'on', or 'upon' in formal writing.

entry_json.avoid: After 'rely on' use a noun or an -ing form: 'rely on receiving help', not 'rely on receive help'.

entry_json.definition: give an account of something you have investigated; the subject examined follows 'on', and the same pattern works for the noun
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The committee will report on the results of the trial in the spring.
example_sentences: Journalists who report on conflict face particular risks.
The document is a report on air quality in six European cities.

contexts.text: The committee will report on the results of the trial in the spring.
Journalists who report on conflict face particular risks.

confusables.difference: Without 'on' it means to state a fact or an incident: 'She reported the theft.' With 'on' it means to study and describe a subject.
'To' names the person or body you answer to: 'She reports to the head of department.'

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse 'report on' with 'report to'. One names the subject, the other names your boss.

entry_json.definition: admiration for somebody, or careful attention to something such as a rule or an environment; the preposition is 'for'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Respect for the environment has to be taught early, not added later as a school subject.
example_sentences: There is enormous respect for teachers in her country.
The company showed little respect for local planning rules.

contexts.text: Respect for the environment has to be taught early, not added later as a school subject.
There is enormous respect for teachers in her country.

confusables.difference: 'Respect to' only appears in the fixed linker 'with respect to', meaning 'concerning'. For admiration it is 'respect for'.
The plural is a fixed formal phrase: 'pay your respects', meaning to attend a funeral or greet someone formally.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'respect of' for admiration. 'In respect of' is legal English meaning 'concerning', which is a different thing entirely.

entry_json.definition: answer, or act because of something that has happened; the preposition is 'to', and it also works for reacting to treatment or to a signal
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The council responded to the complaints by extending the consultation period.
example_sentences: Only 12 per cent of those contacted responded to the survey.
Patients who respond well to the first treatment rarely need the second.

contexts.text: The council responded to the complaints by extending the consultation period.
Only 12 per cent of those contacted responded to the survey.
She responded to my email within an hour.

confusables.difference: 'Answer' takes a direct object with no preposition: 'answer the question'. 'Respond' needs 'to'.
'React' is more immediate and often emotional; 'respond' suggests a considered reply.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'respond the question'. The preposition 'to' is compulsory.

entry_json.definition: cause something to happen; the cause is the subject and the effect follows 'in', which is the opposite arrangement to 'result from'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Heavy rainfall in March resulted in flooding across the low-lying districts.
example_sentences: Cutting the bus service resulted in a sharp rise in car journeys.
The reform resulted in longer waiting lists rather than shorter ones.

contexts.text: Heavy rainfall in March resulted in flooding across the low-lying districts.
Cutting the bus service resulted in a sharp rise in car journeys.

confusables.difference: The arrow points the other way. 'A resulted in B' means A caused B; 'A resulted from B' means B caused A.
minimal_pair: The flooding resulted from the rain.

confusables.difference: 'Cause' takes a direct object: 'The rain caused flooding.' 'Result in' needs the preposition.

entry_json.avoid: Follow it with a noun, not a clause: 'resulted in flooding', not 'resulted in the area flooded'.

entry_json.definition: at this exact moment, or immediately; it strengthens 'now' and normally sits at the end of the clause
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am living with my parents right now while I save for a deposit.
example_sentences: I can't talk right now; can I call you back in ten minutes?
Right now the priority is finishing the first draft.

contexts.text: I am living with my parents right now while I save for a deposit.
I can't talk right now; can I call you back in ten minutes?

confusables.difference: The formal written equivalent, and the right choice in Task 1: 'At present, 40 per cent of homes have solar panels.'
In British English 'just now' can mean a moment ago, in the past. 'Right now' is always the present.

entry_json.avoid: Keep it out of formal writing. Task 1 and Task 2 want 'currently', 'at present' or 'at the time of writing'.

entry_json.definition: an increase in something; as a noun it takes 'in' before the thing that increased, and 'of' before the size of the increase
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The chart shows a steady rise in electricity use across all four countries.
example_sentences: There has been a sharp rise in the number of people working from home.
A rise of twelve per cent was recorded in the final quarter.

contexts.text: The chart shows a steady rise in electricity use across all four countries.
There has been a sharp rise in the number of people working from home.

confusables.difference: 'In' names what rose; 'of' names by how much. 'A rise in prices of 5 per cent' uses both correctly.
'Raise' is a verb needing an object and, in American English, a noun meaning a pay increase. The British noun is 'rise'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'a rise on prices' or 'a rise for prices'. Task 1 examiners see this error constantly; the preposition is 'in'.

entry_json.definition: be used up so that none is left; the thing that is finished is the subject, and no object follows
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We had been walking for four hours when the water ran out.
example_sentences: My phone battery ran out halfway through the journey.
Time ran out before the final question could be answered.

contexts.text: We had been walking for four hours when the water ran out.
Time ran out before the final question could be answered.

confusables.difference: 'Run out' has no object: 'The milk ran out.' 'Run out of' takes one: 'We ran out of milk.' The subject swaps.
Not a possible pattern. Either use 'run out' alone or add 'of'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not put the person first without 'of'. 'I ran out water' is wrong; write 'I ran out of water' or 'The water ran out'.

entry_json.definition: have no more of something left; the person or group is the subject and the supply follows 'of'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I ran out of time in the reading section and guessed the last five answers.
example_sentences: The hospital ran out of beds during the winter peak.
We have run out of milk again.

contexts.text: I ran out of time in the reading section and guessed the last five answers.
The hospital ran out of beds during the winter peak.

confusables.difference: Without 'of' the supply becomes the subject: 'The beds ran out.'
'We're out of milk' describes the state; 'we ran out of milk' describes the moment it happened.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop 'of'. 'I ran out money' is a common slip; the preposition is compulsory.

entry_json.definition: keep money instead of spending it, or spend less than you would otherwise; there is no article before 'money'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cycling to work saves money and takes about the same time as the bus.
example_sentences: Insulating the roof saved us nearly two hundred pounds a year.
Young people find it harder to save money when rents take half their income.

contexts.text: Cycling to work saves money and takes about the same time as the bus.
Young people find it harder to save money when rents take half their income.

confusables.difference: 'Save up' means to collect money over time for a particular purchase: 'saving up for a car'. 'Save money' can also just mean spending less.
minimal_pair: I'm saving up for a car.

confusables.difference: The formal single verb, useful for variety: 'Households have had to economise.'

entry_json.avoid: Do not add an article: 'save money', not 'save the money', unless you mean a specific sum already mentioned.

entry_json.definition: stories set in an imagined future or in space, usually built around science and technology; uncountable, so it takes no article and no plural
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I read a lot of science fiction as a teenager and it is probably why I studied physics.
example_sentences: Science fiction has predicted several technologies that later became ordinary.
The film is science fiction, but the science in it is surprisingly careful.

contexts.text: I read a lot of science fiction as a teenager and it is probably why I studied physics.
Science fiction has predicted several technologies that later became ordinary.

confusables.difference: The informal abbreviation, fine in Speaking, weaker in Task 2 where the full term reads better.
Fantasy uses magic and invented worlds; science fiction works from science and technology. The two are not interchangeable.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'science fictions'. It is uncountable; for one book say 'a science fiction novel'.

entry_json.definition: a program that finds pages on the internet from words you type; a compound noun in which 'search' stays singular
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Most people never look past the first page of results a search engine gives them.
example_sentences: Search engines rank pages by rules that are not published in full.
I use a different search engine at work because it stores less data.

contexts.text: Most people never look past the first page of results a search engine gives them.
I use a different search engine at work because it stores less data.

confusables.difference: A browser is the program you open to view pages; a search engine is the service that finds them. They are not the same thing.
minimal_pair: Type it into a search engine.

confusables.difference: A search engine is one kind of website, but most websites are not search engines.

entry_json.avoid: Keep 'search' singular in the compound: 'search engines', not 'searches engines'.

entry_json.definition: look carefully in order to find something or somebody; 'for' introduces what you want, while 'search' with a direct object means to examine a place or a person
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rescue teams searched for survivors for three days after the earthquake.
example_sentences: I spent an hour searching for a document that was on my desk the whole time.
Students search for sources online before they ever open a library catalogue.

contexts.text: Rescue teams searched for survivors for three days after the earthquake.
Students search for sources online before they ever open a library catalogue.

confusables.difference: Without 'for' the object is the place being examined: 'Police searched the building.' With 'for' it is the thing wanted.
The everyday equivalent. 'Search for' suggests a more systematic or urgent effort.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse the two patterns. 'They searched the survivors' means they examined the survivors' pockets, not that they looked for them.

entry_json.definition: a school for pupils aged roughly eleven to sixteen or eighteen in Britain; used without an article when you mean the stage of education
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I only started studying English seriously at secondary school.
example_sentences: Class sizes in secondary schools have grown faster than in primary schools.
The town has two secondary schools and four primary schools.

contexts.text: Class sizes in secondary schools have grown faster than in primary schools.
I only started studying English seriously at secondary school.

confusables.difference: The American term, also used in some other countries. British English, and most IELTS material, says 'secondary school'.
The stage before, for roughly ages five to eleven.

entry_json.avoid: Drop the article for the stage: 'at secondary school', not 'at the secondary school', unless you mean one specific building.

entry_json.definition: try to do something, especially over a long period or in an official way; it takes a to-infinitive and belongs to formal writing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The policy seeks to reduce car use without making life harder for people outside the city.
example_sentences: This essay seeks to explain why the two studies reached opposite conclusions.
Governments have long sought to encourage saving through tax relief.

contexts.text: The policy seeks to reduce car use without making life harder for people outside the city.
This essay seeks to explain why the two studies reached opposite conclusions.

confusables.difference: 'Try' is the everyday word and fits Speaking. 'Seek to' is formal and would sound stilted in conversation.
minimal_pair: The council is trying to cut traffic.
The policy seeks to cut traffic.

confusables.difference: With a noun object it means to look for or ask for: 'seek advice', 'seek asylum'.

entry_json.avoid: Note the irregular past: seek, sought, sought. 'Seeked' is not a word.

entry_json.definition: begin a journey, or explain something clearly in writing; with 'to' plus a verb it means to start with a particular aim
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The report sets out three options for reducing waste in the county.
example_sentences: We set out early to avoid the traffic on the coast road.
She set out to prove that the original figures were wrong.

contexts.text: The report sets out three options for reducing waste in the county.
We set out early to avoid the traffic on the coast road.

confusables.difference: The explaining sense is separable: 'set the options out'. The journey sense takes no object at all.
For journeys, 'set off' is more common in speech: 'We set off at six.' 'Set out' is slightly more formal.

entry_json.avoid: The verb does not change in the past: set, set, set. 'Setted out' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: start an organisation, arrange an event, or install equipment ready to use; separable, so a pronoun goes in the middle
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She set up a small business selling repaired bicycles two years after graduating.
example_sentences: The university set up a committee to review the marking system.
It took twenty minutes to set the projector up before the talk.

contexts.text: She set up a small business selling repaired bicycles two years after graduating.
The university set up a committee to review the marking system.

confusables.difference: The formal single verb, better in Task 2: 'The charity was established in 1998.'
minimal_pair: They set up the charity in 1998.

confusables.difference: 'Set out' explains or begins a journey; 'set up' creates or installs. Different phrasal verbs entirely.

entry_json.avoid: A pronoun object must split the phrase: 'set it up', never 'set up it'.

entry_json.definition: likely or expected to do something very soon; it follows 'be' and is common in news writing and in predictions
entry_json.own_context_sentence: House prices are set to fall for the first time in a decade.
example_sentences: The new line is set to open in 2027 if funding is approved.
Temperatures are set to rise above thirty degrees by the weekend.

contexts.text: House prices are set to fall for the first time in a decade.
The new line is set to open in 2027 if funding is approved.

confusables.difference: 'Due to' means scheduled for a particular time. 'Set to' means expected, with a little more uncertainty.
minimal_pair: The train is due to arrive at six.

confusables.difference: 'About to' means within minutes; 'set to' can cover months or years.

entry_json.avoid: It needs 'be' in front. Write 'prices are set to rise', not 'prices set to rise', outside a newspaper headline.

entry_json.definition: not having enough of something, or less than a stated figure; it follows 'be' or 'run', and the thing lacking follows 'of'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The hospital is short of nurses, not of equipment.
example_sentences: We were short of time, so the last section of the report was rushed.
Attendance fell just short of the target set in January.

contexts.text: The hospital is short of nurses, not of equipment.
Attendance fell just short of the target set in January.
I was short of money that year, so I lived at home.

confusables.difference: 'Out of' means none at all is left; 'short of' means some remains but not enough.
The noun version: 'a shortage of nurses'. Use it where the sentence needs a noun phrase.
minimal_pair: The hospital is short of nurses.
There is a shortage of nurses.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop 'of'. 'Short staff' means something different: a compound describing staff who are not tall.

entry_json.definition: move from standing to a sitting position; it takes no object, and 'down' cannot be separated from it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Everyone had to sit down on the floor because the hall was full.
example_sentences: Please sit down and we will start in a moment.
He sat down beside me and explained what had gone wrong.

contexts.text: Please sit down and we will start in a moment.
Everyone had to sit down on the floor because the hall was full.

confusables.difference: 'Sit' can describe the state as well as the action: 'He sits at the front.' 'Sit down' is the movement into the chair.
minimal_pair: He sat down at the front.

confusables.difference: 'Seat' is transitive and formal: 'The usher seated us.' 'Sit down' is what you do yourself.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'sit down' with an object. 'Sit down the baby' should be 'sit the baby down' or 'put the baby down'.

entry_json.definition: move or happen more slowly, or make something do so; it works with or without an object, and with an object it is separable
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Economic growth slowed down sharply in the second half of the year.
example_sentences: Traffic slows down at the roundabout, which is why queues form there.
Higher fuel prices slowed the recovery down.

contexts.text: Economic growth slowed down sharply in the second half of the year.
Traffic slows down at the roundabout, which is why queues form there.
I've had to slow down a bit since I started working nights.

confusables.difference: As a verb, 'slow' alone is more formal and common in writing: 'Growth slowed in March.' 'Slow down' is the everyday phrasal version.
One word as a noun: 'a slowdown in growth'. Two words as the verb.
minimal_pair: There was a slowdown in growth.

entry_json.avoid: In Task 1 the single verb is tighter: 'growth slowed' uses fewer words than 'growth slowed down' and reads more academic.

entry_json.definition: in order to do something; a formal purpose linker taking a to-infinitive, and its negative is 'so as not to'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The bus lanes were widened so as to reduce delays at peak times.
example_sentences: She left early so as to avoid the rush hour.
The samples were stored in the dark so as not to affect the results.
collocations: so as not to do sth
with a view to doing sth

contexts.text: The bus lanes were widened so as to reduce delays at peak times.
The samples were stored in the dark so as not to affect the results.

confusables.difference: 'So that' takes a full clause with its own subject: 'so that drivers could pass'. 'So as to' takes only an infinitive and shares the subject.
minimal_pair: so that delays would be reduced

confusables.difference: The same meaning and slightly more common. 'So as to' is especially useful in the negative, where 'in order not to' also works.

entry_json.avoid: The subject must be the same in both halves. 'The lanes were widened so as to drivers save time' is wrong; use 'so that' there.

entry_json.definition: up to the present moment; it pairs naturally with the present perfect because the period is still open
entry_json.own_context_sentence: So far this year the city has recorded its lowest rainfall since records began.
example_sentences: Only three of the twelve councils have responded so far.
So far, so good, though the hardest section is still to come.

contexts.text: So far this year the city has recorded its lowest rainfall since records began.
Only three of the twelve councils have responded so far.
So far I've found the course much easier than I expected.

confusables.difference: A different phrase about extent or distance: 'as far as I know', 'as far as the bridge'. Not about time.
minimal_pair: As far as I know, nothing has changed.

confusables.difference: The formal written equivalent, common in reports: 'Sales to date total £2 million.'

entry_json.avoid: Use it with the present perfect, not the past simple: 'has responded so far', not 'responded so far'.

entry_json.definition: used to introduce a purpose or a result, followed by a full clause with its own subject and verb, often with 'can', 'could' or 'would'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The library extended its opening hours so that students could work later in the evening.
example_sentences: Bins were placed every fifty metres so that visitors would not drop litter.
Write clearly so that the examiner does not have to guess.
collocations: so that sb can do sth
so that sb could do sth

contexts.text: The library extended its opening hours so that students could work later in the evening.
Bins were placed every fifty metres so that visitors would not drop litter.
I set two alarms so that I don't miss the early train.

confusables.difference: 'So that' allows a different subject in the second half; 'so as to' does not.
'So' alone introduces a result, not a purpose: 'It rained, so we stayed in.' 'So that' introduces intention.
minimal_pair: It rained, so we stayed in.
We stayed in so that we could work.

entry_json.avoid: 'That' can be dropped in speech but keep it in writing. Also do not follow it with an infinitive: not 'so that to help'.

entry_json.definition: a way of solving a problem; the problem follows 'to', which is the preposition most candidates get wrong
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is no single solution to traffic congestion in a city built before cars existed.
example_sentences: The report proposes a practical solution to the shortage of student housing.
Recycling is only part of the solution to plastic waste.

contexts.text: There is no single solution to traffic congestion in a city built before cars existed.
The report proposes a practical solution to the shortage of student housing.

confusables.difference: 'For' is possible when you mean a product designed for a market, but with problems the standard preposition is 'to'.
'Answer' also takes 'to'. Both are correct, but 'solution' suits a problem while 'answer' suits a question.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'solution of the problem' in an essay. 'Solution of' belongs to chemistry, where it means a liquid mixture.

entry_json.definition: a thing of a type you cannot name exactly; it takes a singular noun after 'of', usually without an article
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There should be some kind of support for students who are the first in their family to go to university.
example_sentences: The machine made some kind of clicking noise before it stopped.
They want some kind of guarantee before they sign.

contexts.text: There should be some kind of support for students who are the first in their family to go to university.
The machine made some kind of clicking noise before it stopped.

confusables.difference: Interchangeable in British English; 'sort' is very slightly more informal.
'A kind of' points at one example of a category: 'a kind of bread'. 'Some kind of' admits you do not know which.

entry_json.avoid: It signals vagueness, which costs marks in writing. In Task 2 name the thing: 'financial support', not 'some kind of support'.

entry_json.definition: a different person from the one already mentioned; 'else' always follows the pronoun, and the possessive is 'someone else's'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: If I cannot make the meeting, someone else from the team will attend.
example_sentences: The flat had already been let to someone else by the time I called.
It is easy to spend someone else's money.

contexts.text: If I cannot make the meeting, someone else from the team will attend.
The flat had already been let to someone else by the time I called.

confusables.difference: The order is fixed. 'Else' comes second: 'someone else', 'something else', 'somewhere else'.
The neutral written alternative; 'someone else' is more natural in speech and in letters.

entry_json.avoid: The apostrophe goes on 'else', not on 'someone': 'someone else's car', never 'someone's else car'.

entry_json.definition: a different thing from the one mentioned; 'else' follows the pronoun and cannot come before it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: If the first plan fails, we will have to try something else.
example_sentences: I meant to say one thing and something else came out.
There is something else you should know before you decide.

contexts.text: If the first plan fails, we will have to try something else.
There is something else you should know before you decide.

confusables.difference: Not used alone. English says 'something else', or 'some other thing' with a noun.
Use 'anything else' in questions and negatives: 'Is there anything else?' 'Something else' is for statements.

entry_json.avoid: Adjectives also follow the pronoun: 'something useful', 'something else useful'. Never 'useful something'.

entry_json.definition: approximately, before a number, or similar to, before a noun; the meaning depends on what follows
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Something like forty per cent of the students in my class were international.
example_sentences: The journey costs something like fifteen pounds each way.
I want a job something like the one my sister has.

contexts.text: Something like forty per cent of the students in my class were international.
The journey costs something like fifteen pounds each way.

confusables.difference: The formal written equivalent, and the one Task 1 needs: 'approximately 40 per cent'.
A vagueness tag added at the end of a list: 'a sandwich or a salad, something like that.'

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it with figures in Task 1. Examiners want 'approximately', 'just over' or 'around'.

entry_json.definition: a type or category of something, or, as a hedge before an adjective, 'partly'; the noun after 'of' is usually singular with no article
entry_json.own_context_sentence: That sort of question comes up in every Part 3 discussion.
example_sentences: What sort of music do you listen to when you are working?
I was sort of relieved when the interview was cancelled.

contexts.text: What sort of music do you listen to when you are working?
That sort of question comes up in every Part 3 discussion.

confusables.difference: Interchangeable in British English. 'Sort of' is slightly more common in speech in Britain.
'Type' is the most formal of the three and the safest in writing: 'this type of housing'.

entry_json.avoid: The hedging use, 'I was sort of tired', is spoken only, and repeated too often it makes an answer sound uncertain.

entry_json.definition: deal with a problem or organise something that is in a mess; separable, and with a pronoun the split is compulsory
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I need to sort out my accommodation before the term starts.
example_sentences: The bank sorted the problem out within a day, to my surprise.
Give me an hour to sort myself out and I will meet you there.

contexts.text: I need to sort out my accommodation before the term starts.
The bank sorted the problem out within a day, to my surprise.

confusables.difference: The formal single verb for writing: 'The dispute was resolved.' 'Sort out' is conversational.
Without 'out', 'sort' means to arrange into groups: 'sort the papers by date'. With 'out' it means to fix.

entry_json.avoid: Too informal for Task 2. Use 'resolve', 'address' or 'deal with' in an essay.

entry_json.definition: seem, from what you have heard, to be a particular thing; it can also mean to have a similar sound, and it takes a noun or a clause
entry_json.own_context_sentence: That sounds like a good compromise, provided everyone has time to read it first.
example_sentences: It sounds like the flight has been delayed again.
Her accent sounds like my grandmother's.

contexts.text: That sounds like a good compromise, provided everyone has time to read it first.
It sounds like the flight has been delayed again.

confusables.difference: 'As if' plus a clause is the careful written form: 'It sounds as if the flight is delayed.' 'Sound like' plus a clause is common in speech.
minimal_pair: It sounds as if he is unwell.
It sounds like he is unwell.

confusables.difference: With an adjective there is no 'like': 'That sounds good', not 'That sounds like good'.
minimal_pair: That sounds like a good idea.

entry_json.avoid: Do not add 'like' before an adjective. 'It sounds like interesting' is wrong; say 'It sounds interesting'.

entry_json.definition: have a conversation with somebody, often about something specific; British English prefers 'to' where American English often uses 'with'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I need to speak to my tutor about changing the deadline.
example_sentences: Could I speak to the manager, please?
She spoke to the whole department about the changes.

contexts.text: I need to speak to my tutor about changing the deadline.
Applicants should speak to a member of staff before submitting the form.

confusables.difference: Standard in American English and increasingly common elsewhere. British IELTS material uses 'speak to'.
'Talk to' suggests a longer, more informal conversation; 'speak to' can be a brief or official exchange.

entry_json.avoid: Do not omit the preposition. 'Speak the manager' is wrong; 'speak English' is a different pattern, where the object is a language.

entry_json.definition: use a period of time doing something; 'spend' takes time or money as its object, and no preposition follows it directly
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I spend more time commuting than I do cooking, which says something about the city.
example_sentences: Children now spend less time outdoors than any previous generation.
We spent three days in the capital and the rest on the coast.

contexts.text: My grandmother would rather talk on the phone than send a message.
Talking on the phone while driving is illegal in most countries.

confusables.difference: 'By phone' names the method in a formal notice: 'Bookings can be made by phone.' 'On the phone' describes the conversation itself.
minimal_pair: Talk to her on the phone.
Bookings can be made by phone.

confusables.difference: Wrong preposition. It is 'on the phone'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop the article: 'on the phone', not 'on phone'.

entry_json.definition: say what is true; 'the' is fixed here, and 'to tell the truth' also works as a phrase meaning 'to be honest'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Children are more likely to tell the truth when they are not afraid of the punishment.
example_sentences: To tell the truth, I found the second task easier than the first.
He did not tell the truth about how long the work would take.

contexts.text: Children are more likely to tell the truth when they are not afraid of the punishment.
To tell the truth, I found the second task easier than the first.

confusables.difference: Not English. The verb is 'tell': 'tell the truth', 'tell a lie', 'tell a story'.
Possible but literary or dramatic. 'Tell the truth' is the everyday phrase.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop the article. 'Tell truth' is wrong; it is always 'tell the truth'.

entry_json.definition: usually be a particular way, without being so in every case; a hedge that protects a general claim from being disproved by one exception
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cities with good public transport tend to be less polluted than those built around the car.
example_sentences: Older houses tend to be more expensive to heat.
Candidates who read the question twice tend to be more accurate.
collocations: have a tendency to do sth

contexts.text: Cities with good public transport tend to be less polluted than those built around the car.
Older houses tend to be more expensive to heat.

confusables.difference: Almost the same, though 'tend to be' sounds more careful and more academic in an essay.
Same structure with an action verb: 'tend to rise', 'tend to leave'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not add a second hedge. 'Tend to usually be' is redundant; one hedge is enough.

entry_json.definition: do something regularly or usually; it takes a to-infinitive and is the most useful hedging verb in Task 2
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Younger workers tend to change jobs more often than their parents did.
example_sentences: Prices tend to rise in the weeks before a holiday.
People tend to underestimate how long a piece of writing will take.

contexts.text: Younger workers tend to change jobs more often than their parents did.
Prices tend to rise in the weeks before a holiday.
I tend to study better in the morning.

confusables.difference: With 'towards' plus a noun it means to move in a direction: 'The figures tend towards a plateau.'
minimal_pair: The line tends towards a plateau.

confusables.difference: 'Used to' is a past habit that has stopped. 'Tend to' is a present tendency.
minimal_pair: I used to walk to work.
I tend to walk to work.

entry_json.avoid: The negative is 'tend not to do sth', which is more natural than 'do not tend to do sth' in writing.

entry_json.definition: the standard way of expressing gratitude; two words as a phrase, hyphenated only when it works as a noun, as in 'a thank-you note'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Thank you for taking the time to look at my application.
example_sentences: Thank you, that is exactly what I needed.
I would like to say thank you to everyone who helped with the move.

contexts.text: Thank you for taking the time to look at my application.
Thank you, that is exactly what I needed.

confusables.difference: 'Thanks' is the informal short form, fine with friends and colleagues, weaker in a formal letter.
After 'for' use the -ing form: 'thank you for helping', not 'thank you for help me'.

entry_json.avoid: In a formal letter do not end with just 'thanks'. Write 'Thank you for your time' followed by 'Yours sincerely'.

entry_json.definition: a stronger, more formal expression of thanks; 'very much' comes at the end, never between 'thank' and 'you'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Thank you very much for arranging the extension at such short notice.
example_sentences: Thank you very much indeed for all your help this term.
'Here's your change.' 'Thank you very much.'

contexts.text: Thank you very much for arranging the extension at such short notice.
'Here's your change.' 'Thank you very much.'

confusables.difference: Warmer and more personal; 'very much' is slightly more formal and more common in writing.
A brief, semi-formal ending for an email, less formal than 'thank you very much'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not split it: 'Thank you very much', never 'Thank very much you'.

entry_json.definition: because of somebody or something, when the result is good; using it for a bad result sounds sarcastic
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Thanks to the new cycle lanes, journeys across the centre are faster than by car.
example_sentences: Thanks to a scholarship, she was able to finish the degree.
The harvest was saved thanks to two weeks of unexpected rain.

contexts.text: Thanks to the new cycle lanes, journeys across the centre are faster than by car.
Thanks to a scholarship, she was able to finish the degree.

confusables.difference: Neutral about whether the result is good or bad. 'Thanks to' implies gratitude.
minimal_pair: Thanks to the rain, the crops survived.
Because of the rain, the match was cancelled.

confusables.difference: Formal, and traditionally follows a noun or 'be': 'The delay was due to snow.'

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it for a bad outcome unless you intend sarcasm. 'Thanks to the strike, I missed my exam' reads as bitter, not neutral.

entry_json.definition: on the particular day already mentioned; it is the reported-speech version of 'today', and it takes no preposition
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The letter arrived on a Friday, and that day everything changed.
example_sentences: She said she would call, but no call came that day.
We had planned to walk, but it rained all that day.

contexts.text: She said she would call, but no call came that day.
We had planned to walk, but it rained all that day.

confusables.difference: 'Today' is the day you are speaking. 'That day' is a day in the story you are telling.
Adding 'on' is possible for emphasis, but the bare form is more usual: 'that day'.

entry_json.avoid: In reported speech, 'today' becomes 'that day': 'He said he was leaving that day', not 'leaving today'.

entry_json.definition: used to introduce a clearer or more exact restatement of what you have just said; it is followed by a comma in careful writing and often abbreviated to 'i.e.'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The survey covered only adults of working age, that is, those between 18 and 65.
example_sentences: Attendance rose in the second half, that is, after the fee was removed.
The results apply to one city only, that is, they cannot be generalised.

contexts.text: The survey covered only adults of working age, that is, those between 18 and 65.
Attendance rose in the second half, that is, after the fee was removed.

confusables.difference: The longer version, identical in meaning and slightly more formal.
minimal_pair: that is to say, adults over 18

confusables.difference: 'For example' gives one case out of many; 'that is' restates the whole thing more precisely.
minimal_pair: citrus fruit, that is, oranges and lemons

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it to introduce an example. 'That is' means the same thing said again; 'for example' means one of several.

entry_json.definition: used to say that something is finished, that nothing more will follow, or that somebody has got something right
entry_json.own_context_sentence: That's it, we've covered everything on the list.
example_sentences: 'So you turn left at the lights?' 'That's it, then straight on.'
One more paragraph and that's it, the essay is done.

contexts.text: That's it, we've covered everything on the list.
'So you turn left at the lights?' 'That's it, then straight on.'

confusables.difference: 'That's all' means nothing more remains. 'That's it' can also mean 'exactly right'.
The full form is rare in speech and sounds emphatic or annoyed: 'That is it, I'm leaving.'

entry_json.avoid: Never use it in writing. In an essay conclusion write 'In conclusion' or 'To sum up'.

entry_json.definition: the years from 1801 to 1900; centuries take 'the' and an ordinal number, and the preposition before them is 'in'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Most of the terraced housing in the city was built in the 19th century.
example_sentences: Railways transformed travel in the 19th century more than any invention since.
The population of London tripled during the 19th century.

contexts.text: Most of the terraced housing in the city was built in the 19th century.
Railways transformed travel in the 19th century more than any invention since.

confusables.difference: The article is compulsory: 'in the 19th century', never 'in 19th century'.
Used before a noun it is hyphenated and drops 'the': '19th-century architecture'.

entry_json.avoid: Remember the century number is one higher than the years: the 19th century means the 1800s.

entry_json.definition: the years from 1901 to 2000; used with 'in' for the period and with 'of' after 'the first half'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Life expectancy rose by more than thirty years over the course of the 20th century.
example_sentences: Two world wars shaped the first half of the 20th century.
Car ownership became normal in the second half of the 20th century.

contexts.text: Life expectancy rose by more than thirty years over the course of the 20th century.
Car ownership became normal in the second half of the 20th century.

confusables.difference: 'The 1900s' usually means the decade 1900 to 1909, so it is not a safe substitute for the century.
'Last century' is relative to now and can confuse a reader in a hundred years. Name the century in academic writing.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop the article. It is 'in the 20th century', never 'in 20th century'.

entry_json.definition: the years from 2001 to 2100; the ordinal is 'twenty-first', and the phrase takes 'in' or 'of'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The main environmental challenge of the 21st century is not producing energy but storing it.
example_sentences: Skills that mattered in the 20th century are not always the skills of the 21st century.
Cities in the 21st century are growing faster than at any point in history.

contexts.text: The main environmental challenge of the 21st century is not producing energy but storing it.
Cities in the 21st century are growing faster than at any point in history.

confusables.difference: The article is required: 'in the 21st century'.
Shorter and clear in speech, but 'the 21st century' is precise and better in writing.

entry_json.avoid: Write the ordinal correctly: 21st, not 21th. The pattern is 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 21st, 22nd, 23rd.

entry_json.definition: the disadvantages of something; the topic follows 'about', and this is the plain spoken version of 'the drawbacks'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: One of the bad things about living in the centre is that nothing is ever quiet.
example_sentences: The bad things about working from home only appeared after a few months.
There are good things and bad things about studying in a second language.

contexts.text: One of the bad things about living in the centre is that nothing is ever quiet.
The bad things about working from home only appeared after a few months.

confusables.difference: The formal written equivalent, and the one Task 2 wants: 'the drawbacks of remote working'.
Note the preposition changes: 'things about', but 'disadvantages of'.

entry_json.avoid: Keep it out of Task 2. Examiners reward 'drawbacks', 'disadvantages' or 'negative consequences' over 'bad things'.

entry_json.definition: the most enjoyable or most useful aspect of something; often followed by 'about' plus the topic, or by a relative clause
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The best thing about the course was meeting people from other departments.
example_sentences: The best thing I ever bought was a second-hand bicycle.
For me the best thing is being able to walk to work.

contexts.text: The best thing about the course was meeting people from other departments.
For me the best thing is being able to walk to work.

confusables.difference: Adding 'to do' turns it into advice about action: 'The best thing to do is wait.'
minimal_pair: The best thing is the location.
The best thing to do is wait.

confusables.difference: The formal written version for Task 2.

entry_json.avoid: It takes 'about', not 'of': 'the best thing about the course', never 'the best thing of the course'.

entry_json.definition: the most sensible course of action; it is usually followed by 'is' plus a bare infinitive, without 'to'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The best thing to do is book the ticket early and accept that plans might change.
example_sentences: When you cannot answer a question, the best thing to do is move on and come back.
The best thing to do would be to speak to your tutor directly.
collocations: the best thing to do is...

contexts.text: When you cannot answer a question, the best thing to do is move on and come back.
The best thing to do would be to speak to your tutor directly.

confusables.difference: Without 'to do' it names a feature, not an action.
minimal_pair: The best thing is the price.
The best thing to do is wait.

confusables.term: it is best to do sth
confusables.difference: The tighter written form: 'It is best to book early.'

entry_json.avoid: After 'is', the bare infinitive is normal: 'the best thing to do is book', not 'is to book' in speech, though both are accepted.

entry_json.definition: a superlative frame: 'the best' plus a noun, then 'in' plus the area compared; superlatives take 'in' with places, not 'of'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The library is said to be the best collection of maps in the country.
example_sentences: It is the best hospital in the country for that particular operation.
She was the best player in the league that season.

contexts.text: It is the best hospital in the country for that particular operation.
She was the best player in the league that season.

confusables.difference: Superlatives take 'in' with places and groups: 'the best in the world', 'the tallest in the class'.
Safer than a bare superlative, because it is much harder to disprove.
minimal_pair: the best hospital in the country
one of the best hospitals in the country

entry_json.avoid: A bare superlative is a strong claim. In Task 2 hedge it: 'one of the best' or 'among the best'.

entry_json.definition: the true situation; used in fixed patterns such as 'this is the case', 'if that is the case' and 'as is the case with'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: This is often the case in cities where housing has been treated as an investment.
example_sentences: If that is the case, the figures in the second table must be wrong.
As is the case with most surveys, the response rate was low.
collocations: as is the case with sth

contexts.text: This is often the case in cities where housing has been treated as an investment.
As is the case with most surveys, the response rate was low.
If that's the case, I'd rather take the train.

confusables.difference: A completely different phrase meaning as a precaution: 'Take an umbrella in case it rains.'
minimal_pair: If that is the case, we should act.
Take a coat in case it rains.

confusables.difference: Means 'anyway' and introduces a further point: 'In any case, the deadline has passed.'

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse 'if that is the case' with 'in case'. The first refers back to a fact, the second prepares for a possibility.

entry_json.definition: how far or how much something is true; a formal frame taking a full clause after 'which', and often the opening of a Task 2 response
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The essay examines the extent to which car use can be reduced without new taxes.
example_sentences: Opinion differs on the extent to which schools should teach values.
The extent to which the results can be generalised is unclear.

contexts.text: The essay examines the extent to which car use can be reduced without new taxes.
The extent to which the results can be generalised is unclear.

confusables.difference: The question form, which is how many Task 2 prompts are written: 'To what extent do you agree?'
minimal_pair: To what extent do you agree?
the extent to which I agree

confusables.difference: The plain everyday version. 'The extent to which' is the academic register.

entry_json.avoid: Follow it with a full clause, not a noun: 'the extent to which prices rose', not 'the extent to which of prices'.

entry_json.definition: used to turn a whole clause into a noun phrase so it can be the subject or object of a sentence; the clause after 'that' keeps its normal word order
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The fact that the scheme was never evaluated makes it impossible to judge.
example_sentences: Nobody disputes the fact that the population is ageing.
The fact that she had no formal training did not stop her.

contexts.text: The fact that the scheme was never evaluated makes it impossible to judge.
Nobody disputes the fact that the population is ageing.

confusables.difference: A long way of saying 'because'. Examiners see it constantly; the shorter word is usually better.
minimal_pair: due to the fact that it rained

confusables.difference: The correct way to follow 'despite' with a clause, since 'despite' itself needs a noun.
minimal_pair: despite the fact that it rained

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it just to add words. 'Due to the fact that' should almost always be 'because'.

entry_json.definition: the thing that comes before all others in time or importance; often followed by a relative clause with no relative pronoun
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The first thing you notice about the city is how quiet the centre is.
example_sentences: The first thing to check is whether the form has been signed.
The first thing I look for in a flat is natural light.

contexts.text: The first thing you notice about the city is how quiet the centre is.
The first thing to check is whether the form has been signed.

confusables.difference: 'First of all' is a linker opening a list of points. 'The first thing' is a noun phrase and needs a verb after it.
minimal_pair: First of all, consider the cost.
The first thing to consider is the cost.

confusables.difference: 'At first' means in the beginning, before things changed: 'At first I found it hard.'

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it as a linker on its own. 'The first thing, the cost is high' is not a sentence; you need 'is'.

entry_json.definition: a narrative opener naming your first action in a story; the relative pronoun is left out, and 'was' is followed by a bare infinitive
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The first thing I did when I arrived was find somewhere to live.
example_sentences: The first thing I did after the exam was sleep for ten hours.
The first thing I did was call my parents to tell them the news.
collocations: the first thing I did was...

contexts.text: The first thing I did when I arrived was find somewhere to live.
The first thing I did after the exam was sleep for ten hours.

confusables.term: the first thing I did was to...
confusables.difference: Both 'was find' and 'was to find' are correct. The bare infinitive is more natural in speech.
minimal_pair: The first thing I did was find a flat.
The first thing I did was to find a flat.

confusables.difference: 'Firstly' organises an argument; 'the first thing I did' tells a story. Part 2 needs the second.

entry_json.avoid: Keep the past tense throughout: 'The first thing I did was call', not 'was to calling' or 'was called'.

entry_json.definition: used to mark an event that has never happened before; usually preceded by 'for' and paired with the present perfect
entry_json.own_context_sentence: For the first time in history, more people live in cities than in the countryside.
example_sentences: For the first time in history, the majority of new cars sold were electric.
It was the first time in history that the tournament had been cancelled.
collocations: for the first time in history

contexts.text: For the first time in history, more people live in cities than in the countryside.
For the first time in history, the majority of new cars sold were electric.

confusables.difference: Without 'in history' the claim is much smaller and safer: 'for the first time since 2010'.
minimal_pair: for the first time in history

confusables.difference: The single formal adjective: 'an unprecedented rise'. Useful when you want the idea without the long phrase.

entry_json.avoid: It is a very strong claim. Use it only where you are sure; otherwise write 'for the first time in decades'.

entry_json.definition: the day after the one being described; the written narrative equivalent of 'tomorrow' in reported speech
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The storm passed overnight and the following day the roads were clear again.
example_sentences: She submitted the application on Monday and heard back the following day.
The results were published the following day.

contexts.text: The storm passed overnight and the following day the roads were clear again.
She submitted the application on Monday and heard back the following day.

confusables.difference: Almost identical. 'The following day' is slightly more formal and more common in written narrative.
'Tomorrow' is relative to now. In a story about the past, use 'the following day'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not mix 'tomorrow' into a past narrative. Once you are in the past, it must be 'the following day'.

entry_json.definition: used before a noun to introduce a list or an item that comes next in the text; it can also stand alone before a colon
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The following factors were considered: cost, location and travel time.
example_sentences: Applicants must provide the following documents before the interview.
The following table shows the results for each of the four cities.

contexts.text: The following factors were considered: cost, location and travel time.
Applicants must provide the following documents before the interview.

confusables.difference: 'As follows' comes after the verb and before a colon: 'The reasons are as follows:'. 'The following' comes before a noun.
The time meaning, about the next day, is a separate use of the same word.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'the followings'. 'Following' is an adjective here and never takes a plural s.

entry_json.definition: the advantages of something; the topic follows 'about', and this is the everyday spoken version of 'the benefits'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: One of the good things about a small town is that you know your neighbours.
example_sentences: The good things about the job outweigh the long hours.
There are good things about both systems.

contexts.text: One of the good things about a small town is that you know your neighbours.
The good things about the job outweigh the long hours.

confusables.difference: The written equivalent, and note the preposition changes to 'of': 'the benefits of exercise'.
Also takes 'of'. This is the phrase Task 2 questions themselves use.

entry_json.avoid: In Task 2 write 'the benefits' or 'the advantages'. 'Good things' reads as A2 vocabulary in a B2 essay.

entry_json.definition: the aspect that matters most; usually followed by 'is' plus a clause or an infinitive, and used to focus attention
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The important thing is that the data was collected the same way in both years.
example_sentences: The important thing is not to panic when you cannot hear a word.
The important thing about the diagram is the direction of the arrows.

contexts.text: The important thing is that the data was collected the same way in both years.
The important thing is not to panic when you cannot hear a word.

confusables.difference: The superlative claims there is only one. 'The important thing' is softer and easier to defend.
minimal_pair: The most important thing is preparation.

confusables.difference: A neater cleft alternative that shows more range: 'What matters is consistency.'

entry_json.avoid: Follow it with 'is'. 'The important thing, preparation' is not a sentence.

entry_json.definition: the most recent occasion; it introduces a clause with no preposition and normally takes the past simple
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The last time I took a test like this I ran out of time on the final section.
example_sentences: The last time the river flooded was in 2007.
When was the last time you read a book for pleasure?

contexts.text: The last time the river flooded was in 2007.
When was the last time you read a book for pleasure?

confusables.difference: Without 'the' it works as an adverb: 'Last time I was late.' With 'the' it is a noun phrase: 'the last time I was late'.
minimal_pair: The last time I was late was in March.

confusables.difference: A separate phrase meaning finally, after a long wait.

entry_json.avoid: Do not add a preposition: 'the last time I went', not 'in the last time I went'.

entry_json.definition: the single thing that matters more than all others; a superlative frame followed by 'is' plus a clause or an infinitive
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The most important thing in the writing paper is answering the question that was actually asked.
example_sentences: For most families the most important thing is a school within walking distance.
The most important thing to remember is that the graph shows percentages, not totals.

contexts.text: The most important thing in the writing paper is answering the question that was actually asked.
For most families the most important thing is a school within walking distance.

confusables.difference: Without 'most' the claim is softer and safer.
minimal_pair: The most important thing is cost.

confusables.difference: A tighter linker with the same emphasis: 'Above all, the essay must answer the question.'

entry_json.avoid: Use it once at most in an essay. Two things cannot both be the most important, and a marker will notice.

entry_json.definition: the day after the one in the story; used in past narrative, and it takes no preposition
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We arrived late at night and the next day walked the whole length of the old town.
example_sentences: He promised to send the file and it arrived the next day.
The next day everything looked more manageable.

contexts.text: We arrived late at night and the next day walked the whole length of the old town.
He promised to send the file and it arrived the next day.

confusables.difference: Without 'the' it appears mainly in fixed phrases like 'next-day delivery'.
'Tomorrow' looks forward from now; 'the next day' looks forward from a point in the past.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'tomorrow' inside a past-tense story. Once the narrative is in the past, use 'the next day'.

entry_json.definition: the opposite side of a named thing, or, figuratively, the opposing view; the noun follows 'of'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The industrial estate is on the other side of the railway from the housing.
example_sentences: There is a footbridge to the other side of the motorway.
It is worth hearing the other side of the argument before deciding.
collocations: the other side of the road
the other side of the argument

contexts.text: The industrial estate is on the other side of the railway from the housing.
It is worth hearing the other side of the argument before deciding.

confusables.difference: Almost identical and slightly more formal, useful in Task 1 map descriptions.
minimal_pair: the other side of the road
the opposite side of the road

confusables.difference: The linker for contrasting ideas. 'The other side of the argument' is a noun phrase; 'on the other hand' is a connector.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop 'of' before the noun: 'the other side of the road', not 'the other side the road'.
