entry_json.headword: the other side of the world
entry_json.ipa: ði ˌʌðə saɪd əv ðə ˈwɜːld
entry_json.definition: a place very far away, often another continent; used loosely rather than geographically, and usually with 'on' or 'to'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My sister lives on the other side of the world and we speak more now than when she lived here.
example_sentences: Fruit is flown from the other side of the world so that it can be sold out of season.
Moving to the other side of the world at nineteen was harder than I expected.
collocations: on the other side of the world
from the other side of the world

chunk.pattern: the other side of the world

contexts.text: Fruit is flown from the other side of the world so that it can be sold out of season.
contexts.gap_span: the other side of the world

contexts.text: My sister lives on the other side of the world and we speak more now than when she lived here.
contexts.gap_span: the other side of the world

confusables.difference: 'Abroad' just means another country. 'The other side of the world' stresses enormous distance.
minimal_pair: She works on the other side of the world.

confusables.difference: The neutral formal word, better in Task 2: 'overseas suppliers'.

entry_json.avoid: It is figurative, so avoid it in Task 1 where you should give the actual region or country.

entry_json.definition: the part that remains; the verb agrees with what follows 'of', so 'the rest of the group are' but 'the rest of the money is'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The first section takes half the time; the rest of the paper has to fit into what is left.
example_sentences: The rest of the students had already gone home.
I spent the rest of the afternoon rewriting the introduction.
collocations: for the rest of my life

contexts.text: The first section takes half the time; the rest of the paper has to fit into what is left.
The rest of the students had already gone home.

confusables.difference: 'The others' stands alone and means the remaining people or things: 'The others had left.'
minimal_pair: The rest of the group left.

confusables.difference: The verb 'rest' means to relax. The noun 'the rest' means the remainder. Same spelling, unrelated meanings.

entry_json.avoid: Make the verb agree with the noun after 'of': 'the rest of the students were', 'the rest of the money was'.

entry_json.definition: all the other countries apart from the one being discussed; it takes a singular verb
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The country produces more solar power per person than the rest of the world combined.
example_sentences: What happens to that region's water supply matters to the rest of the world.
The pandemic showed how quickly one place can affect the rest of the world.
collocations: compared with the rest of the world

contexts.text: The country produces more solar power per person than the rest of the world combined.
What happens to that region's water supply matters to the rest of the world.

confusables.difference: 'The whole world' includes the country you are talking about; 'the rest of the world' excludes it.
An adverb or adjective, useful for compressing: 'sales worldwide'.

These days I read far less than I used to.

What do you think of the new library building?

confusables.difference: 'Think about' is extended consideration; 'think of' is a single moment of recall or invention.

It rained heavily this afternoon and the match was called off.

entry_json.definition: during the evening of today; it takes no preposition and is normally used with a future or a present form

The results will be announced this evening.

entry_json.avoid: No preposition is needed: 'this evening', not 'in this evening'.

This kind of question comes up in almost every listening section.

This summer was the hottest since records began in that region.

confusables.difference: Never with a preposition.

This time last year the same street was completely flooded.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'in this time'. That would mean within this period, which is a different idea.

contexts.text: I am going to see my family this weekend for the first time since March.
This weekend the museum is free for local residents.

confusables.difference: British English uses 'at the weekend' for the general habit; American English uses 'on the weekend'. 'This weekend' needs neither.
Never with a preposition.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'in this weekend' or 'on this weekend'. The phrase stands alone.

The figures for this year are not yet complete.

contexts.text: Applications have risen by almost a fifth this year.
This year I finally started swimming regularly.

confusables.difference: No preposition is used with 'this'. 'In 2019' takes 'in'; 'this year' does not.

entry_json.avoid: While the year is still going, use the present perfect: 'have risen this year', not 'rose this year'.

Support should go first to those who need it most.

Thousands of students apply for a few hundred places every year.

entry_json.avoid: Never say 'turn on it'. Pronouns sit between the verb and the particle.

entry_json.definition: increase the volume, heat or power of something; separable, and with a pronoun the object must sit in the middle
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Could you turn the heating up? The office is freezing.
example_sentences: He turned the radio up so that he could hear it in the kitchen.
Turn it up a little; I cannot hear the announcement.

contexts.text: Could you turn the heating up? The office is freezing.
He turned the radio up so that he could hear it in the kitchen.

confusables.difference: The opposite: to reduce volume or heat. 'Turn down' also means to refuse an offer.
Without an object it means to arrive, often unexpectedly: 'He turned up an hour late.'

entry_json.avoid: A pronoun object always splits the phrase: 'turn it up', never 'turn up it'.

entry_json.definition: not able to do something; it follows 'be' and takes a to-infinitive, and it is the formal written negative of 'can'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Many households were unable to heat their homes properly last winter.
example_sentences: The committee was unable to reach a decision at the first meeting.
Patients who are unable to travel can be seen at home.

contexts.text: Many households were unable to heat their homes properly last winter.
Patients who are unable to travel can be seen at home.

confusables.difference: The everyday equivalent. 'Unable to' is more formal and fits an essay or a letter of complaint.
minimal_pair: They are unable to afford it.

confusables.difference: 'Unable to' describes one specific limit. 'Disabled' describes a person's long-term condition, and the two should not be used loosely.

entry_json.avoid: It needs 'be' in front and 'to' plus a verb after: 'is unable to attend', not 'unable attending'.

entry_json.definition: facing a difficulty or an opponent that is hard to beat; it follows 'be' or 'come', and the difficulty follows 'against'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Small independent shops are up against chains that can afford to sell at a loss.
example_sentences: We were up against a deadline that could not be moved.
Anyone applying for that scholarship is up against several hundred others.

contexts.text: Small independent shops are up against chains that can afford to sell at a loss.
We were up against a deadline that could not be moved.

confusables.difference: The formal single verb for writing: 'Independent shops face competition from chains.'
'Against' alone means opposed to an idea: 'I am against the plan.' 'Up against' means struggling with an obstacle.

entry_json.avoid: It is informal. In Task 2 write 'face', 'contend with' or 'are confronted by'.

entry_json.definition: moving repeatedly in both directions, or, of a figure, rising and falling without a clear trend; the word order is fixed
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The figures went up and down throughout the period, with no clear trend in either direction.
example_sentences: He walked up and down the platform waiting for the delayed train.
My marks were up and down all year until I changed how I revised.

contexts.text: The figures went up and down throughout the period, with no clear trend in either direction.
He walked up and down the platform waiting for the delayed train.

confusables.difference: The single academic verb Task 1 rewards: 'The figures fluctuated between 20 and 30 per cent.'
Not English. The order is fixed as 'up and down', like 'back and forth'.

entry_json.avoid: In Task 1 prefer 'fluctuated' or 'varied'. 'Up and down' is accurate but reads as A2 vocabulary.

entry_json.ipa: ˌʌp tə ˈsɪksti maɪlz pər ˈaʊə
entry_json.definition: a model of 'up to' plus a maximum figure; it states a ceiling, not the usual value, and it comes directly before the number
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The turbines can operate in winds of up to 60 miles per hour before they shut down.
example_sentences: The train reaches speeds of up to 60 miles per hour on the straighter sections.
Gusts of up to 60 miles per hour were recorded along the coast.

contexts.text: The train reaches speeds of up to 60 miles per hour on the straighter sections.
Gusts of up to 60 miles per hour were recorded along the coast.

confusables.difference: 'Up to' gives a maximum; 'at least' gives a minimum. Confusing them reverses the claim.
'About' is an estimate around the figure; 'up to' is a ceiling never exceeded.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'up to' for a typical value. 'Speeds of up to 60 mph' does not mean it usually travels at 60.

entry_json.definition: the responsibility or the decision of a particular person; it follows 'be', and the person comes after 'to'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is up to each student to check the reading list before the first seminar.
example_sentences: 'Shall we go by train or drive?' 'It's up to you.'
Whether the scheme continues is up to the council, not the residents.
collocations: it is up to sb to do sth

contexts.text: It is up to each student to check the reading list before the first seminar.
'Shall we go by train or drive?' 'It's up to you.'

confusables.difference: With a number, 'up to' means a maximum. With a person, it means responsibility. Same words, different job.
'It depends on you' means you are the deciding factor; 'it's up to you' means you get to choose.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'up to me' in a formal essay. Write 'it is the responsibility of' or 'the decision rests with'.

entry_json.definition: as far as a limit, or as many or as much as a maximum; before a number it states a ceiling, and before a point it means as far as that point
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The offer applies to households earning up to thirty thousand pounds a year.
example_sentences: The hall holds up to four hundred people.
Up to this point the argument is convincing.

contexts.text: The hall holds up to four hundred people.
The offer applies to households earning up to thirty thousand pounds a year.

confusables.difference: With a person after it, the phrase means responsibility instead: 'It's up to her.'
A fixed hedge meaning partly: 'I agree up to a point.' Very useful in Speaking Part 3.

entry_json.avoid: 'Up to 50 per cent off' means the discount may be much smaller. Do not read a ceiling as a typical figure.

vocab_new.lemma: verbs, compounds, collocations, prepositional phrases and other common fixed phrases.

entry_json.headword: verbs, compounds, collocations, prepositional phrases and other common fixed phrases.
entry_json.definition: Not a phrase to learn. This line is a fragment of the Oxford Phrase List's own description of what the list contains, which was picked up as an entry when the list was extracted from the source document. It is kept here only so that the block matches its worklist exactly.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The Oxford Phrase List covers idioms, phrasal verbs, compounds, collocations, prepositional phrases and other common fixed phrases.
example_sentences: The heading explains that the list contains phrasal verbs, compounds, collocations, prepositional phrases and other common fixed phrases.
Each of the categories named in that heading is taught separately elsewhere in this deck.

chunk.pattern: verbs, compounds, collocations, prepositional phrases and other common fixed phrases.

contexts.text: The Oxford Phrase List covers idioms, phrasal verbs, compounds, collocations and other common fixed phrases.
Learners are usually taught collocations and phrasal verbs as separate categories.

confusables.difference: A collocation is a partnership of words that native speakers habitually use together, such as 'heavy rain'. It is one of the categories this line names.
A phrasal verb is a verb plus a particle whose meaning is not predictable from the parts, such as 'give up'. It is another of the categories named.

entry_json.avoid: Do not study this row as English. It is an extraction artefact from the source list's own front matter, and it should be removed or replaced by an editor rather than learned.

entry_json.definition: stay where you are or delay acting until somebody or something arrives; 'for' is compulsory before the person or thing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I waited for the bus for nearly forty minutes in the rain.
example_sentences: Patients often wait for months to see a specialist.
We are waiting for the results before deciding anything.
collocations: wait for sb to do sth

contexts.text: I waited for the bus for nearly forty minutes in the rain.
Patients often wait for months to see a specialist.

confusables.difference: Not possible. English always uses 'wait for' before the thing awaited.
'Expect' takes a direct object and means to believe something will come: 'I expect a reply.' 'Wait for' is about the time you spend.
minimal_pair: I am waiting for a reply.

entry_json.avoid: Never drop 'for'. 'Wait me' is one of the most common errors at A1 and A2, and it persists into higher levels.

entry_json.definition: stop sleeping, or make somebody stop sleeping; without an object it describes you waking, and with one it is separable
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I wake up at half past six whether I set an alarm or not.
example_sentences: The noise from the road woke me up three times last night.
Try to wake up at the same time every day, even at weekends.

contexts.text: I wake up at half past six whether I set an alarm or not.
The noise from the road woke me up three times last night.

confusables.difference: 'Wake up' is opening your eyes; 'get up' is leaving the bed. They can be an hour apart.
With a pronoun object the phrase must split: 'wake me up', never 'wake up me'.

entry_json.avoid: Note the irregular past: wake, woke, woken. 'Waked' is not used in British English.

entry_json.definition: the typical pattern of living of a person or a community, including habits, values and work; it is countable, so it takes 'a' or a possessive
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cheap flights changed the way of life of small island communities within a generation.
example_sentences: Farming is not just a job in that region; it is a way of life.
Their traditional way of life has survived three centuries of change.

contexts.text: Cheap flights changed the way of life of small island communities within a generation.
Farming is not just a job in that region; it is a way of life.

confusables.difference: 'Lifestyle' is an individual's chosen habits, often about health or spending. 'Way of life' is broader and usually collective.
That phrase is about money and material comfort; 'way of life' is about culture and habits.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'way of live'. The noun is 'life'; 'live' is the verb.

entry_json.definition: a greeting to somebody arriving at a place or joining a group; 'to' introduces the place, and no verb is needed
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Welcome to the department; your supervisor will meet you at eleven.
example_sentences: Welcome to Manchester, where the weather is exactly as advertised.
Welcome to the team, and do ask if anything is unclear.

contexts.text: Welcome to the department; your supervisor will meet you at eleven.
Welcome to Manchester, where the weather is exactly as advertised.

confusables.difference: A different fixed phrase, used to answer thanks, not to greet somebody.
As a verb it takes a direct object with no preposition: 'The school welcomes new students.'

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'welcome in London'. The preposition is 'to' for the place you are arriving at.

entry_json.definition: familiar to many people; hyphenated as 'well-known' before a noun and written as two words after the verb
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is well known that regular exercise reduces the risk of heart disease.
example_sentences: She is a well-known architect in the region.
The building is well known locally but rarely visited by tourists.

contexts.text: It is well known that regular exercise reduces the risk of heart disease.
She is a well-known architect in the region.

confusables.difference: 'Famous' is stronger and usually about a wide public. 'Well known' can be limited to one field or one area.
The word order is fixed. 'Well known' is the compound adjective; 'known well' sounds like an adverb describing how you know something.

entry_json.avoid: Hyphenate before a noun and not after the verb: 'a well-known writer', but 'the writer is well known'.

vocab_new.lemma: when it comes to doing sth

entry_json.headword: when it comes to doing sth
entry_json.definition: used to introduce the particular activity you are about to discuss; the 'to' is a preposition, so the verb after it takes the -ing form
entry_json.own_context_sentence: When it comes to reducing emissions, changing how people travel matters more than changing what they buy.
example_sentences: When it comes to choosing a university, reputation is only one factor.
When it comes to writing under time pressure, planning saves more time than it costs.
collocations: when it comes to doing sth
as far as sth is concerned

chunk.pattern: when it comes to doing sth

contexts.text: When it comes to reducing emissions, changing how people travel matters more than changing what they buy.
When it comes to choosing a university, reputation is only one factor.

confusables.term: when it comes to do sth
confusables.difference: A very common error. The 'to' here is a preposition, so it must be followed by -ing.
With a noun after 'to' the meaning is the same: 'when it comes to money'.

entry_json.avoid: Never follow it with an infinitive. 'When it comes to reduce emissions' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: as far as a particular subject is concerned; a topic-introducing frame taking a noun after 'to'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: When it comes to public transport, the two cities are barely comparable.
example_sentences: When it comes to cost, the second option is clearly better.
Attitudes differ enormously when it comes to homework.

contexts.text: When it comes to public transport, the two cities are barely comparable.
Attitudes differ enormously when it comes to homework.

confusables.term: when it comes to doing sth
confusables.difference: With a verb after 'to' you need the -ing form.
minimal_pair: when it comes to cutting costs

confusables.difference: A shorter topic marker with a similar job: 'As for cost, the second option is better.'

entry_json.avoid: Do not overuse it as a paragraph opener. Two in one essay is enough, or it becomes a verbal tic.

entry_json.definition: used to say that something is true in both cases, or to introduce an indirect question where both outcomes matter; 'or not' can follow 'whether' immediately or come at the end
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Whether or not the funding is approved, the survey work will go ahead.
example_sentences: The report examines whether or not the policy achieved its stated aim.
I will finish the course whether I enjoy it or not.

contexts.text: Whether or not the funding is approved, the survey work will go ahead.
The report examines whether or not the policy achieved its stated aim.

confusables.difference: 'If' works for a simple indirect question: 'I asked if she was coming.' Only 'whether' can take 'or not' directly, and only 'whether' can follow a preposition.
minimal_pair: I asked whether or not she was coming.
I asked if she was coming.

confusables.difference: Without 'or not' it still introduces two possibilities, but it loses the emphasis that both cases are covered.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'if or not'. That combination is not English; use 'whether or not'.

entry_json.definition: concerning; a formal topic marker taking a noun after 'to', and note that 'regard' is singular in this phrase
entry_json.own_context_sentence: With regard to the second question, the evidence points in the opposite direction.
example_sentences: I am writing with regard to the invoice dated 3 March.
With regard to cost, both proposals are within budget.

contexts.text: With regard to the second question, the evidence points in the opposite direction.
I am writing with regard to the invoice dated 3 March.

confusables.difference: A very common error. 'Regards' with an s belongs at the end of a letter: 'Kind regards'. The phrase is 'with regard to'.
A shorter single-word alternative with the same meaning and register.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'with regards to'. The singular 'regard' is the only correct form in this phrase.

entry_json.definition: concerning a particular aspect; a formal marker used in academic and technical writing to narrow what you are comparing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: With respect to energy use, the two buildings perform very differently despite their similar size.
example_sentences: The two groups were matched with respect to age and income.
With respect to the first objective, the project succeeded.

contexts.text: With respect to energy use, the two buildings perform very differently despite their similar size.
The two groups were matched with respect to age and income.

confusables.difference: 'Respect for' is admiration for a person. 'With respect to' is a topic marker and has nothing to do with politeness.
A fixed spoken phrase used before disagreeing with somebody, and it usually signals that disagreement is coming.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it in Speaking. It sounds like a legal document; in conversation say 'as for' or 'when it comes to'.

entry_json.definition: apart from; a formal way of excluding one item from a general statement, and the noun follows 'of'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: With the exception of Norway, every country in the sample increased its rail spending.
example_sentences: All the buildings on the site are new, with the exception of the church.
With the exception of one participant, everyone completed the full programme.

contexts.text: With the exception of Norway, every country in the sample increased its rail spending.
All the buildings on the site are new, with the exception of the church.

confusables.difference: The everyday equivalent, shorter and just as accurate: 'except for Norway'.
A different structure taking a clause: 'The rules are the same, with the exception that fees are waived.'

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'with exception of'. The article is compulsory: 'with the exception of'.

entry_json.definition: have a particular job; 'as' introduces the role, and the job title takes an article in the singular
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She worked as a nurse for eleven years before moving into training.
example_sentences: I worked as a waiter while I was studying.
He works as an engineer for a company that builds bridges.

contexts.text: She worked as a nurse for eleven years before moving into training.
I worked as a waiter while I was studying.

confusables.difference: 'In' names the field or the place: 'work in education', 'work in an office'. 'As' names the job title.
'For' names the employer: 'work for the council'.

entry_json.avoid: Use an article before a singular job: 'work as a nurse', not 'work as nurse'.

entry_json.definition: be employed by a person or an organisation; 'for' names the employer, and the same phrase can mean 'to be effective for somebody'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: He has worked for the same housing association since he left university.
example_sentences: I work for a small firm that designs lighting for theatres.
Studying late at night works for some people and not for others.

contexts.text: He has worked for the same housing association since he left university.
Studying late at night works for some people and not for others.

confusables.difference: 'With' names colleagues you work alongside; 'for' names the employer or the boss.
minimal_pair: I work with three other designers.

confusables.difference: 'As' names the job title, not the employer.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'work in' for a company name. It is 'work for the BBC', or 'work at the BBC' for the location.

entry_json.definition: put a lot of effort into your work; 'hard' is the adverb here, and adding -ly changes the meaning completely
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Students who work hard in the first term find the second one far easier.
example_sentences: She worked hard for three years to qualify.
Working hard is not the same as working long hours.

contexts.text: Students who work hard in the first term find the second one far easier.
She worked hard for three years to qualify.

confusables.difference: 'Hardly' means almost not. 'He works hardly' means he barely works, which is the opposite of what you mean.
The noun phrase: 'It was hard work.' The adverb phrase is 'work hard'.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'work hardly' when you mean effort. This single letter reverses the meaning of your sentence.

entry_json.definition: spend time producing or improving something; 'on' introduces the project or the skill being developed
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I need to work on my pronunciation more than on my grammar.
example_sentences: The team has been working on the design for eighteen months.
Engineers are working on a system that stores heat underground.

contexts.text: I need to work on my pronunciation more than on my grammar.
Engineers are working on a system that stores heat underground.

confusables.difference: 'Work at' emphasises persistent effort on a skill: 'She works at her accent every day.' 'Work on' is broader.
'For' names the employer, not the task.

entry_json.avoid: After 'on' use a noun or an -ing form: 'work on improving it', not 'work on improve it'.

entry_json.definition: calculate an amount, or find the answer to a problem by thinking; separable, and with a pronoun the object must sit in the middle
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It took me a while to work out how much the trip would actually cost.
example_sentences: Work the total out before you agree to the contract.
I could not work it out until somebody showed me the formula.

contexts.text: It took me a while to work out how much the trip would actually cost.
Work the total out before you agree to the contract.

confusables.difference: Without an object it means to exercise, or to end well: 'I work out twice a week.' 'It worked out in the end.'
minimal_pair: I work out at the gym.

confusables.difference: The formal single verb, better for Task 1: 'The figure was calculated from the raw data.'

entry_json.avoid: A pronoun object always splits the phrase: 'work it out', never 'work out it'.

entry_json.definition: do a task jointly with other people; it takes no object, and the people involved can be added with 'with'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Departments that work together produce better results than those that compete for the same budget.
example_sentences: We worked together on the presentation and split it in half.
Countries have to work together on problems that cross borders.

contexts.text: Departments that work together produce better results than those that compete for the same budget.
We worked together on the presentation and split it in half.

confusables.difference: The formal single verb for Task 2: 'Universities collaborate on research.'
Adding 'with' is possible but can sound redundant; 'work with' alone is usually enough.

entry_json.avoid: Do not put an object straight after it. 'Work together the plan' is wrong; write 'work together on the plan'.

entry_json.definition: act jointly in order to achieve a stated goal; 'for' introduces the aim, expressed as a noun
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Neighbouring councils worked together for a shared solution to the flooding.
example_sentences: Charities and hospitals worked together for better care in rural areas.
The two countries have worked together for decades on air quality.
collocations: work together for a common goal

contexts.text: Neighbouring councils worked together for a shared solution to the flooding.
Charities and hospitals worked together for better care in rural areas.

confusables.difference: 'For' takes a noun goal; 'to' takes a verb. Both express purpose.
minimal_pair: work together to bring about change

confusables.difference: 'On' names the project or the subject; 'for' names the aim.

entry_json.avoid: Be careful: 'have worked together for decades' uses 'for' to mean duration, not purpose. Context decides which it is.

entry_json.definition: act jointly in order to achieve something; 'to' plus an infinitive expresses the purpose
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Governments will have to work together to reduce emissions, because pollution ignores borders.
example_sentences: Local groups worked together to save the last cinema in the town.
Researchers from four universities worked together to build the model.

contexts.text: Governments will have to work together to reduce emissions, because pollution ignores borders.
Local groups worked together to save the last cinema in the town.

confusables.difference: 'For' takes a noun; 'to' takes a verb. The meaning is the same.
minimal_pair: work together to find a solution

confusables.difference: Not idiomatic. Use the infinitive of purpose or 'on' plus a noun.

entry_json.avoid: Use the infinitive, not 'for' plus a verb. 'Work together for reduce emissions' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: do your job alongside particular people or a particular group; 'with' names colleagues or the people you serve, not your employer
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I work with a small team of four, which means everyone knows what everyone else is doing.
example_sentences: She works with children who have missed a lot of school.
It is easier to work with people whose strengths differ from your own.

contexts.text: I work with a small team of four, which means everyone knows what everyone else is doing.
She works with children who have missed a lot of school.

confusables.difference: 'For' names your employer or boss; 'with' names your colleagues or the people you help.
A slightly more formal alternative stressing that you work in parallel rather than as a team.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'with' for your employer. 'I work with Sony' suggests you are a partner, not an employee.

entry_json.definition: anxious about somebody or something; it follows 'be' or 'get', and the cause of the worry follows 'about'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Many parents are worried about how much time their children spend on screens.
example_sentences: I was worried about the speaking test until I did a practice one.
Residents are worried about the effect the new road will have on air quality.

contexts.text: Many parents are worried about how much time their children spend on screens.
I was worried about the speaking test until I did a practice one.

confusables.difference: 'Worried' describes the person who feels it; 'worrying' describes the thing that causes it.
minimal_pair: I am worried about the results.

confusables.difference: The formal written equivalent, and the better choice in Task 2.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse 'worried' with 'worrying'. Saying 'I am worrying about the news' is possible but 'I am worrying' as an adjective is not.

entry_json.definition: a polite way of saying what you want; it takes a noun or a to-infinitive, and it is more polite than 'want'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I would like to apply for the position advertised on your website.
example_sentences: I would like a return ticket to Edinburgh, please.
Would you like to join us for lunch?

contexts.text: I would like to apply for the position advertised on your website.
Would you like to join us for lunch?

confusables.difference: 'I like coffee' is a permanent preference. 'I would like a coffee' is a request for one now.
'Want' is direct and can sound rude in a request. 'Would like' is the polite standard.

entry_json.avoid: It takes the infinitive, not the -ing form: 'I would like to go', never 'I would like going'.

entry_json.definition: would very much like to do something; warmer and more enthusiastic than 'would like', and it takes a to-infinitive
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I would love to visit Japan, mainly because of the rail network.
example_sentences: I would love to take a year out, but I cannot afford it.
'Come for dinner on Saturday.' 'I'd love to, thanks.'

contexts.text: I would love to visit Japan, mainly because of the rail network.
'Come for dinner on Saturday.' 'I'd love to, thanks.'

confusables.difference: 'Would love' is stronger and warmer. 'Would like' is neutral and works in formal writing.
'I love travelling' is a general habit. 'I would love to travel' is a wish about a specific occasion.
minimal_pair: I would love to travel next year.

entry_json.avoid: It is enthusiastic and personal, so keep it for Speaking and informal letters. Task 2 wants 'it would be beneficial to'.

entry_json.definition: would prefer to do something; it takes a bare infinitive, with no 'to', and the comparison uses 'than' plus another bare infinitive
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I would rather live in a small flat near the centre than a large house an hour away.
example_sentences: Most people would rather pay a little more than wait three weeks for delivery.
I would rather you did not mention it before the meeting.

contexts.text: I would rather live in a small flat near the centre than a large house an hour away.
Most people would rather pay a little more than wait three weeks for delivery.

confusables.difference: 'Prefer' takes 'to' plus an infinitive and can be followed by 'rather than': 'I prefer to walk rather than drive.'
When the subject changes, the second verb goes into the past tense even though the meaning is present: 'I would rather you came tomorrow.'

entry_json.avoid: No 'to' after 'would rather': 'I would rather stay', never 'I would rather to stay'.

entry_json.definition: record something on paper so that it is not forgotten; separable, and with a pronoun the split is compulsory
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Write the reference number down before you close the page.
example_sentences: I write down every new phrase I meet and review the list on Sundays.
She wrote it down on the back of a receipt.

contexts.text: Write the reference number down before you close the page.
I write down every new phrase I meet and review the list on Sundays.

confusables.difference: Almost identical and slightly more formal: 'Note down the main points.'
The formal single verb, better in a report: 'The temperature was recorded every hour.'

entry_json.avoid: A pronoun object always goes in the middle: 'write it down', never 'write down it'.

entry_json.definition: used to ask or say what problem somebody or something has; it usually appears after 'something', 'nothing' or 'what'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is something wrong with the heating; it only works in two rooms.
example_sentences: What is wrong with the argument is that it assumes everyone has a car.
There is nothing wrong with asking for help.

contexts.text: There is something wrong with the heating; it only works in two rooms.
What is wrong with the argument is that it assumes everyone has a car.

confusables.difference: 'Wrong about' means mistaken in an opinion: 'He was wrong about the date.' 'Wrong with' names a fault.
minimal_pair: He was wrong about the date.
Something is wrong with the clock.

confusables.difference: As a plain adjective it means incorrect: 'the wrong answer', 'the wrong platform'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'wrong in the heating'. The preposition for a fault is 'with'.

entry_json.definition: used in conversation to introduce an explanation the listener does not yet have; a discourse marker, not a real question about seeing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I could not take the earlier train, you see, because the meeting overran.
example_sentences: You see, the problem is that the two systems do not talk to each other.
I grew up by the sea, you see, so I have never learned to drive.

confusables.difference: 'As you can see' points at something visible, such as a chart, and is fine in a presentation.
minimal_pair: As you can see from the graph...

confusables.difference: A vaguer filler with no explaining function. 'You see' at least introduces a reason.

entry_json.avoid: Never write it in Task 1 or Task 2. It addresses a listener directly, which academic writing does not do.
